lessons.title: The DPperformance Philosophy
lessons.summary: What we believe, why we coach this way, and how we differ from contest prep or generic gym coaching.
lessons.body:
**What DPperformance actually is**

DPperformance is a lifestyle-first online coaching service. Our clients are professionals, parents, business owners, expats, students, and people who already have full lives. They want to look better, feel stronger, and trust the structure of a real plan — but they will not, and should not, blow up their week to chase a physique. The job of a DPperformance coach is to deliver structured progress without breaking the rest of someone's life.

That sentence is the lens for every decision in this course. If a recommendation is "technically optimal" but it requires a client to weigh fish at a wedding, refuse a friend's birthday cake, or do fasted cardio at 4:30am because their plan has no flex, it is the wrong recommendation for our model. There are coaches who specialise in that — we are not them, and we are not trying to be.

**Lifestyle-first coaching**

Lifestyle-first means coaching that bends without breaking. Clients have weddings, holidays, work travel, sick kids, late nights, and bad weeks. Our plans assume that. We build:

- Meal-structured plans the client can actually run on a Tuesday and a Saturday
- Travel options, eat-out swaps, and named "easier" days for high-stress weeks
- Step targets and cardio levels that fit the client's actual schedule, not a fantasy one
- Communication that anticipates real-life friction instead of being surprised by it

When something disrupts the plan, we don't shame, we adjust. The client keeps moving. That is the DPperformance experience.

**Adherence beats perfection — every time**

Clean Health, Layne Norton, and every credible coach in the space agree on one thing: the best diet is the one the client will actually follow. We take that further. We design specifically so the client can follow it. A 90% adherent client on a 350-calorie deficit will out-progress a 60% adherent client on a 600-calorie deficit, every time. Our defaults are graduated and conservative for a reason — they leave headroom so adherence stays high.

Practical examples:

- We do not push hunger higher than necessary. If progress is on track, calories hold.
- We do not stack a deficit, low sleep, high cardio, and a stressful week on top of each other. We pick the lever that matters most.
- We do not punish a missed workout. We adjust forward and rebuild the week.

**Structured plans + flexibility within structure**

This is where we deliberately diverge from much of the wider industry. Many systems "graduate" intermediate clients into IIFYM — flexible dieting where the client tracks macros and chooses their own meals freely. We don't. Every DPperformance client gets a 3+2 (or similar) meal-structured plan, regardless of how experienced they are. Why:

- Adherence is higher when the next meal is already decided
- Decision fatigue is the #1 quiet killer of long-term plans
- Clients come to us for an answer, not a calorie budget

Inside that structure we are very flexible — swaps, eat-out options, travel kits, named easier days. Flexibility lives **inside** the structure, not instead of it.

**The macros exception.** If a client specifically asks to track macros instead of following a structured plan, we don't refuse — but the deal is conditional. They get the macro target, and they show us the logs. We monitor results. If progress stalls, our first move is to gently steer them back into a meal plan because we know decision fatigue is usually the cause. If after that conversation they still push hard for macros, we respect their autonomy and let them run it. We don't argue people into a system they don't want — we just stay accountable for the result, and we keep the door open to swap back if it's not working.

**Multi-system pluralism**

We have a default DP system (3+2 meal-structured, animal-protein-anchored, controlled carb cycling), but we are not religious about it. Coaches learn the default plus alternative frameworks: keto, intermittent fasting, vegan, Mediterranean, isocaloric, low-carb, and paleo. When a client's lifestyle, religion, ethics, or biology genuinely doesn't fit the default, we adapt the system to the client — never force the client into the system. The flag here is "genuine fit" — not novelty or trend chasing.

**Results without rigidity**

What a DPperformance client will get:
- A real, structured plan with named meals, swaps, training, cardio and steps
- A coach who replies thoughtfully, predicts what comes next, and sees them as a person
- Progress they can sustain — typically 5–10 kg over a 12-week cut, then a planned reverse
- Education they can keep — what their body did and why

What we will not ask of them:
- Aggressive deficits beyond the graduated cap, even on request
- Cardio over the weekly ceiling, even on request
- Pushing a deficit through multi-week symptoms — sleep, mood, performance, or adherence drops mean step out, not push through
- Anything that puts results above their physical or mental health

**How we differ from contest prep and generic gym coaching**

Two ends of the spectrum bracket where we sit. On one end is contest prep — extreme depletion, peak weeks, water and sodium manipulation, posing, federations. That world is its own sport, with coaches trained for it. We are not those coaches. On the other end is generic gym coaching — a PDF program, occasional WhatsApp tips, no real check-ins, no real plan. That model is too thin to actually move the needle for someone with a life.

DPperformance sits in the structured middle: a real, written plan; a real coach who reads every check-in; a real progression through phases; and a real respect for the client's actual schedule. That middle is where the durable physique work happens.

**What success looks like for a DPperformance client**

A real, visible transformation. The scale moved, the photos changed, the lifts went up — and the client still has a life. A 12-week cut down 6 kg with their social life, relationships, and job intact, and the discipline to repeat it next year if they want to — that is a DPperformance success.

Lifestyle-first does not mean soft. Transformations are the game. We are not running a wellness retreat. Clients pay us to deliver visible physical change, and we hold them — and ourselves — to that bar. The lifestyle frame just means we deliver that change without burning the client's existence to the ground in the process. It is genuinely harder than coaching someone who has nothing else going on, because we have to engineer real adherence inside real life.

The wrong success is a client who hit a scale number but burned out, lied on check-ins, hated training, or never wants to coach again. That's a system failure regardless of the photo. The other wrong success is a client who "felt great" and "loved the experience" but didn't actually transform — that's also a system failure, regardless of how nice the relationship was. Hold both edges. We are coaching, not babysitting.

**The frame to carry into the rest of the Academy**

Every later module — nutrition, training, cardio, check-ins, edge cases — is taught against the same lens. When you're deciding whether to push calories down another 100, the questions are: *Will it move the result? Can the client adhere to it without their life unravelling?* If both are yes, push. If only one is yes, hold. When you're tempted to add a fourth cardio session, same test. The lens is constant: drive the transformation, protect the life. We optimise for both — never just one.

lessons.title: Coaching Language & Rapport
lessons.summary: How we talk to clients. Tone, energy, the "wizard" principle, hunger script, and the 10 core language rules.
lessons.body:
**Why language is the product**

Clients don't see your spreadsheet. They don't read your training notes. They experience your coaching almost entirely through written and spoken language. If the plan is a 9 and the language is a 4, they will quit. If the plan is a 7 and the language is a 9, they will stay for years. Language is not the wrapper around the coaching — for the client, it **is** the coaching. Treat it that way.

This lesson is the canonical source for how DPperformance coaches communicate. Every rule below is non-negotiable. The point of putting it here is to make sure you can recall the rules, recognise them in your own messages, and edit yourself before you hit send.

**1. Energy & presence**

Coaches must be encouraging, friendly, engaged, positive, and use future-facing language (assume the client is staying forever). Even if you have 50 clients, they only have one of you. A flat, transactional reply tells the client you are tired of them — even when you aren't. Match the energy you want them to bring to their training and check-ins.

Avoid: robotic tone, boring delivery, low-energy responses, casually mentioning "minimum terms" or hinting their program is ending. None of those produce retention.

**2. Be human**

Use humour where natural. Share a small anecdote when it fits. Notice the client as a person — their job, their dog, the wedding they mentioned six weeks ago. Clients want to impress their coach. That's a feature of the relationship, not a problem. Reinforce it.

**3. No harsh or negative language**

Never shame, never criticise harshly, never say they're doing badly. Instead: encourage, redirect, show how to improve. Tone is supportive authority — not soft, but never cold. "You missed three sessions this week" is information, not a verdict. The follow-up is "let's pick the two that matter and reset Monday."

**4. The "wizard" principle — be the expert who saw it coming**

This is the single highest-leverage technique in DPperformance coaching. Before the client experiences something, you tell them it's coming and how it will feel. Then it arrives. Then they trust you completely.

Example — introducing rest-day calories:
> "You might feel a bit hungrier on rest days — that's normal. It just means we're creating a slightly bigger deficit on those days to keep fat loss moving. By the third rest day this should feel routine."

When the client feels hungry on Tuesday and remembers you predicted exactly that, you stop being a person sending them a meal plan and become an expert who knows what their body is about to do. Adherence and retention both rise.

Use this for: phase transitions, hunger spikes, late-cut flatness, reverse-diet weight gain, deload weeks, post-holiday rebound, female cycle phases. Anything you can predict, predict it before it happens.

**5. Future mapping**

Clients need direction, endpoints, and timeline clarity. They are not motivated by "let's see how we go." They are motivated by "we have 4 weeks left of this cut, then we move into the build."

Example:
> "We've got about 4 weeks left of this cut. Let's push hard to around 51 kg, then we'll start the reverse — carbs come back up and you'll feel stronger, more energised, and start filling out the muscles again. I know the cut feels tough right now, but you're doing so well — let's finish strong, then we move into the building phase."

Always have a near horizon (this week / this phase) and a far horizon (this block / this year) ready.

**6. Normalising phase feelings**

Late cut: empathise with flat look, low pumps, slower PBs. Reframe: "this is normal and means fat loss is nearly complete." Reverse / bulk start: highlight strength rebound, fuller muscles, returning energy. Build excitement for what comes next, not anxiety about what just ended.

**7. The hunger explanation script**

This is one of the most-copied language patterns in the company. Memorise it.

> "Think about it this way — when you eat, your body wants to use all of that food for energy first. Hunger starts when your body has used it all but still wants more energy. It likes to make you hungry, because that means it doesn't have to go into its energy stores — your fat. So having the discipline to push through a bit of hunger means it's going to take that energy from somewhere — and that's going to be your fat stores."

This script works because it reframes hunger from a failure signal into a progress signal. Use it the first time a client reports hunger in a deficit. Reuse it whenever the topic comes back up.

**8. Introducing harder phases**

Always pair the hard thing with the why and the timeline. "We're cutting cardio days to 5 next week — that's the bigger push for these last 4 weeks of the cut." Never drop a harder ask without context. Clients can do hard things; they cannot do mysterious hard things.

**9. The rapport principle**

Rapport is not optional, it is the entire delivery mechanism. Without rapport: adherence drops, retention drops, results drop. Clients stay with coaches they trust and connect with. Rapport is built in tiny consistent acts — remembering the dog's name, asking about the holiday, matching the energy when they hit a PB, sitting with them when they have a hard week. None of these scale on their own. All of them compound.

**10. The 10 core language rules**

The complete checklist. Every weekly reply should be readable against this list.

Always:
1. **Encourage** — find the real win and name it specifically
2. **Explain** — never give a directive without a reason
3. **Predict** — say what's coming before they feel it (the wizard rule)
4. **Guide** — give the next step, not just the diagnosis
5. **Empathise** — acknowledge what's hard before fixing it

Never:
6. **Shame** — no version of "you should have done better"
7. **Criticise harshly** — feedback can be sharp; tone never can
8. **Be robotic** — copy-pasted replies are felt, not read
9. **Be cold** — short isn't the problem, distant is
10. **Be impersonal** — use their name, their context, their previous check-in

**Three more language patterns worth memorising**

In addition to the hunger script, these patterns come up weekly. Memorising them frees up cognitive bandwidth for the actual coaching call.

The "scale noise" reframe — when a client panics over a 0.6 kg overnight rise:
> "That's not fat — fat doesn't move that fast. What you're seeing is water, glycogen, sodium, and gut content shifting around the underlying trend. The trend is what we coach to. Let's look at the 7-day average and the photos."

The "phase transition" frame — when moving from cut to reverse:
> "We're closing the cut and moving into the reverse. Carbs come back up over the next 3–4 weeks. You'll feel stronger, see better pumps, and start filling back out. The scale will move up — that's expected and good. We're rebuilding capacity for the next push."

The "missed week" reset — when a client has a bad week and is bracing for criticism:
> "Bad week happens. Don't carry it into Monday. We restart the structure — three sessions, the meal plan, the steps target. By Wednesday this week looks like every other week."

Notice the pattern: every script names what the client is feeling, explains what's actually happening, and points forward to the next concrete action. That is the DNA of DPperformance coaching language.

**Self-check before sending**

Before you send any non-trivial reply, scan it once for: encourage, explain, predict, guide, empathise. If three of those five are missing, the reply isn't done yet. This is the difference between competent and excellent — and excellent is what keeps a client for two years instead of two months.

lessons.title: The Coach-Client Relationship
lessons.summary: Trust, expectations, communication cadence, escalation paths, and what drives client retention.
lessons.body:
**The shape of the relationship**

A DPperformance coach-client relationship is bounded, structured, and personal. Bounded — there are clear channels, clear response times, and a clear scope of what coach and client owe each other. Structured — every week has a check-in, every check-in has a reply, every reply has a Loom. Personal — inside that structure, the relationship is warm, specific, and remembers details. Get all three right and clients stay for years.

This lesson covers the explicit expectations you set at onboarding, the channels you use, the cadence of communication, when to escalate, and what actually drives retention.

**The three non-negotiables (set in the welcome video)**

Every new client watches a welcome Loom in their first week. That Loom sets three non-negotiables that frame the entire program:

1. **Log your workouts.** Every set, every rep, every weight. The training log is the source of truth for progression. Without it, the coach is guessing.
2. **Hit your daily habits.** Steps target, sleep window, water, daily food structure. These are the levers that move the scale week to week.
3. **Submit your weekly check-in on time.** This is the meeting. Without it, coaching cannot happen.

These three are non-negotiable. Everything else is negotiable inside the plan. Set them firmly and warmly in the welcome message and reference them when adherence slips.

**Communication channels**

DPperformance runs a hub-and-spoke model with a single channel:

- **WhatsApp group** containing the **client + their coach + Daniel.** Daniel is silent by default but visible — the client knows he's there. This is the only channel for client-facing communication.

What goes in WhatsApp:
- Quick questions, daily check-ins, training-day updates
- Photos for substitution requests, gym setup questions
- Soft accountability ("just finished session 3 of 4 this week")

What goes in the formal weekly check-in (in-app form, not WhatsApp):
- Body weight, photos, measurements
- Training adherence, sleep, hunger, mood scores
- Coach-facing notes on the week

The rule: small noise in WhatsApp, signal in the check-in. Clients will sometimes try to do their entire check-in in chat. Redirect them — kindly, the first time; firmly, by the third.

**Response time expectations**

Set clearly at onboarding and held to:

- **Acknowledge within 12 hours.** Even if you can't reply in full, send a quick "got this — coming back to you as soon as I can." Acknowledgement is half of the felt response time.
- **Full reply within 24 hours at the latest — ideally within 12.** A complete, considered response, Loom-led with the actual coaching content. For more in-depth questions where you need to think it through, still inside 24 hours.
- **Urgent / safety**: anything medical or safety-related is handled as soon as possible and escalated to Daniel the same day.

**The weekly check-in reply**

Every reply has the same skeleton (taught in detail in Module 5):
1. Open with one specific detail from their actual check-in (proves you read it)
2. Win callout — name a specific positive
3. Read of the data — what's actually happening
4. Decision — hold or change, with the reason
5. Next-week actions — concrete, fewer than five
6. Forward look — where this fits in the bigger plan (the wizard principle)

Standard length: ~180 words written, or 5–8 minute Loom. Longer when there's a real shift; shorter is fine when the week is a hold.

**When to escalate to Daniel or Angus**

Coach autonomy ends at four hard lines. Inside these lines, escalate inside 24 hours with a 3–5 line summary:

1. **Refunds** — any refund request, partial or full. Never agree on the spot.
2. **Medical or safety concerns** — injury that may need a doctor, mental health flags, suspected disordered eating, anything that puts the client's wellbeing in your hands.
3. **Disputes** — client unhappy with the program in a way that feels structural, not adjustable. "I think this isn't working" is an escalation, not a defence.
4. **Anything outside scope** — see Lesson 1.4 for the full list (contest prep, PEDs, eating disorders, hormones, etc).

Escalation is not weakness. It is the system working. The fastest way to lose a client is to make a unilateral call on something that wasn't yours to decide.

**Communication that retains clients**

Retention is not built on big moments — it's built on a hundred small ones. The biggest drivers, in order:

- **Rapport** — the client likes you and trusts you. Built in tiny acts of attention over time (Lesson 1.2).
- **Results** — visible progress, named in their words. The check-in reply must surface progress they can feel.
- **Future mapping** — they know what's next. The principle: every check-in should leave the client with a clear picture of the next 4 weeks and a vague picture of the next 12. Direction is more motivating than data. Module 6 Lesson 6.2 covers this in depth.
- **Predictability** — the wizard principle. They felt hungry on rest days; you said they would.
- **Recovery from friction** — when you mess up (and you will), how you handle it is what they remember.

**Friction recovery**

When something goes wrong on your side — a late reply, a wrong macro adjustment, a missed Loom — own it cleanly. Acknowledge → name what you'll do differently → move forward. Do not over-apologise. Over-apologising signals fragility; clean ownership signals competence. One sentence is usually enough: "My fault — I'll have the full reply with you by tomorrow morning."

**The relationship over time**

A 12-week client is a transaction. A 12-month client is a relationship. The shift happens around month 3, when the client has lived through one full cycle (cut → reverse, or build → mini-cut). They have direct, embodied evidence that you can predict their body and respect their life. From that point, retention compounds. The work is to get them through those first 12 weeks intact, kept, and bought-in. Everything in this lesson is in service of that.

lessons.title: What We Don't Do
lessons.summary: Scope boundaries. The areas DPperformance coaches refer out, and why those lines exist.
lessons.body:
**The line between scope and out-of-scope**

A DPperformance coach is a lifestyle physique coach. That is a real, defined craft — and it has edges. Outside those edges live other professionals: stage prep coaches, hormone clinicians, physiotherapists, dietitians, sport psychologists, GPs, mental health professionals. The job here is not to be all of those people. The job is to know exactly where our scope ends and to refer out cleanly when a client crosses it.

Coaches who blur these lines hurt clients. The reasoning is the same in every case below: lifestyle coaching ethics plus risk management. We are not insured, trained, or set up to operate outside scope, and pretending otherwise is how clients (and coaches) get hurt.

**1. Contest prep / stage prep — refer to a competition coach**

If a client wants to compete in a bodybuilding, bikini, or physique show, we do not peak them. Stage prep is a different sport. It involves: depletion and refeed protocols, water and sodium manipulation, peak-week practice, posing, tan, suit, federation logistics, and a level of physiological extremity that has no overlap with our lifestyle-first model. We may continue lifestyle-physique work in parallel with a comp coach, but we do not lead a stage peak.

The script: "Stage prep is genuinely a different sport from what we do — I don't want to half-do it for you. I'd rather refer you to a proper comp coach for the prep itself, and we keep the off-season lifestyle work humming alongside it."

**2. PEDs, peptides, hormonal manipulation — refer to a hormone clinic**

We do not advise on, prescribe, or coach around performance-enhancing drugs, peptides, SARMs, anabolic steroids, or hormonal manipulation of any kind. If a client is using or asking about these, the conversation is: refer to a properly licensed hormone clinic, do not change the program around their use, and flag it to Daniel.

This is not a moral position — it's a scope and legal one. We are not clinicians. Programming around exogenous hormones requires medical training we do not have.

**3. Eating disorders — refer to GP, dietitian, or sport psych**

This is the most important boundary in the list. If a client shows signs of disordered eating, we do not treat it. We notice it, we name it gently (or escalate to Daniel to handle the conversation), and we refer to qualified support — typically a GP first, then a registered dietitian and/or sport psychologist with eating-disorder experience.

Signs to notice:
- Skipping meals to "save calories"
- Severe restriction outside the prescribed plan
- Compulsive cardio or punitive training after eating
- Severe weight or body-shape preoccupation that goes beyond normal physique focus
- Self-induced vomiting, laxative use, or any binge/purge pattern
- Sudden secrecy around food or weight

When you see these patterns, do not pretend you didn't. Escalate to Daniel within 24 hours with a short summary. Daniel will lead the referral conversation. The coach's role is to be warm, non-judgemental, and supportive — not therapeutic.

**4. Medical conditions outside scope — refer**

PCOS, thyroid dysregulation, IBS, diabetes (any type), pregnancy and post-partum, hypertension, and any chronic illness all sit outside coach scope. We can absolutely coach a client who has these conditions managed by their actual medical team — but we do not adjust their programming around their pathology. We work to the medical team's parameters. If a client doesn't have a medical team and the condition is active, the first step is a referral to a GP.

**5. Aggressive deficits beyond Q1 graduated cap**

Even if a client requests it. The graduated deficit cap (1.2–1.5 kg/wk for >25–30% body fat, tapering to ~1 kg/wk as they lean out, conservative DP rate for lean clients) is a system rule, not a negotiation. Clients sometimes want to go faster — usually before a holiday, wedding, or photoshoot. The answer is structured education: explain why faster doesn't work, predict what would happen if we did it, offer the alternative (push to the cap, then sustain through the event). This is the wizard principle applied to scope.

**6. Cardio over the weekly ceiling**

Same logic. Even if a client requests more cardio, we don't go past the weekly ceiling. Reasons: recovery debt, injury risk, and the fact that more cardio without higher calories is a worse trade than tightening the food side. We coach the lever, we don't multiply the levers.

**7. Pushing a deficit through multi-week symptoms**

We don't impose a hard week cap on cuts — most lifestyle clients don't need one. What we do impose is a duty to step out when the data says step out. If sleep, mood, training performance, or adherence drops across two or three consecutive weeks despite a sensible plan, the answer is a planned diet break, not a deeper deficit and a longer push. Clients sometimes want to "just push through" — when symptoms are stacking, that's the moment a coach earns their fee by saying no, holding the line, and protecting the back half of the result. The exception that *does* warrant scheduled breaks is the very long cut: clients targeting 20 kg+ of loss carry a cumulative load that genuinely needs structured pauses (typically every 8–10 kg lost, or every 3–4 months in deficit), regardless of week-to-week symptoms. That's planning, not gatekeeping.

**Why these boundaries exist**

Two reasons, both equally weighted:

1. **Ethics of lifestyle coaching.** Our model is built on bending without breaking. The boundaries above all describe situations where bending isn't appropriate — the client needs proper medical, psychological, or specialist help. Pretending we can provide it is a breach of the trust they extended to us.
2. **Risk management.** Every boundary above is also a liability boundary. A coach who runs a comp prep without qualifications, treats an eating disorder, or programs around PEDs is exposing themselves and the company to serious risk. The boundaries protect coaches as much as clients.

**The default move when in doubt**

Escalate. A 3–5 line summary to Daniel, inside 24 hours, every time. There has never been a case where the right move was to handle a scope-edge situation alone. That is the entire point of the system.

options: Lifestyle-first, adherence-driven, transformations as the bar
Maximum results, optimisation over lifestyle
Bodybuilding methodology adapted for general population
Calorie counting and rigid consistency, no exceptions

options: Run the prep yourself — it's good for your portfolio
Refuse to coach them and end the relationship
Run a modified, less aggressive version of contest prep
Refer to a competition coach for the stage prep, continue lifestyle work alongside

questions.q: Which set lists all three of the non-negotiables you set in the welcome video?
options: Macro tracking, daily check-ins, weekly Loom from coach
Standing weekly call, daily Loom from client, training frequency
Logging workouts, daily habits, weekly check-in submission
Calorie tracking, weekly weigh-in, monthly photos

options: We never allow macro tracking under any circumstances

Default is structured plans for everyone — decision fatigue kills adherence. If a client specifically asks for macros, we allow it conditionally (logs required) and steer back to a meal plan if results stall
All experienced clients automatically graduate to IIFYM after 12 weeks
Macros are reserved for clients with 5+ years of training experience

questions.q: A client finishes a 12-week block. They felt amazing, loved the experience, kept engaged — but didn't actually transform visibly. By our standards this is:
options: A success — relationship and engagement matter more than the photo
A system failure — we deliver visible transformation, not just experience. Loved-it-but-didn't-change is a failed coaching outcome
Acceptable — we're a lifestyle business so results are optional
Up to the client alone to decide whether it was a success

questions.q: A client messages at 10pm Saturday with a frustrated, vague "I don't think this is working." Best first move?
options: Reply immediately and defend the program point by point
Quietly offer a partial refund to keep them onside
Pause their program until Monday so they can think
Acknowledge within 12 hours, ask one clarifying question, escalate to Daniel within 24 hours

questions.q: A client shows a clear pattern of skipping meals to "save calories" and punishing herself with cardio after eating. What do you do?
options: Notice it, escalate to Daniel inside 24 hours, do not attempt to treat it yourself
Praise the discipline and tighten her macros further
Cancel her program immediately
Wait two more weeks and see if the pattern resolves on its own

questions.q: When do we deviate from the default nutrition system to an alternative (keto, IF, vegan, Mediterranean, etc.)?
options: Whenever a client mentions they're bored of the food
Automatically after 8 weeks on the default plan
When the client's lifestyle, biology, or beliefs genuinely don't fit the default — never for novelty
Only if Daniel personally approves each deviation

questions.q: Which of the following is OUTSIDE coach autonomy and must be escalated?
options: A 5% calorie adjustment after a stalled week
A client requesting a partial refund mid-block
A swap from incline DB press to incline machine press
Adding a deload week after performance drops

questions.q: A client is in week 14 of a cut, still adherent, sleep good, training strong, scale moving. What do you do?
options: Force a 1–2 week diet break — 12 weeks is the hard cap
Continue the cut — there is no fixed week ceiling; breaks are triggered by symptoms (sleep, mood, performance, adherence drops), not the calendar
Push harder — accelerate the deficit while it is working
Move them straight to maintenance regardless of progress

lessons.title: Energy Needs & Setting Starting Calories
lessons.summary: TDEE estimation, the DP rule of thumb, when to use the calculator, and how to set training-day vs rest-day calories at the start of a block.
lessons.body:
**The job in week one**

Every new client needs a starting number. That number is the spine of the program — calories, macros, meal plan, deficit pacing, and every later adjustment all hang off it. Get it roughly right and the first 4 weeks of coaching are easy. Get it wrong and you spend a month chasing the scale, the client loses confidence, and the build never finds its rhythm. The good news is "roughly right" is genuinely all you need. The body will tell us what's actually true inside two weeks of data. Your job is to give it a sensible starting point.

**The DPperformance rule of thumb**

The DP working starting points every coach should know cold:

- **Average male, 75–85 kg, average height: ~2200 kcal**
- **Average female, 55–65 kg, average height: ~1750 kcal**

These are starting calorie targets for fat loss in an average-activity client — not maintenance, not bulks. They assume 3–5 training days a week, a 10k step daily target, and no extreme outliers. For roughly 70% of new clients, these numbers are within 100–150 kcal of correct. That's close enough — the first check-in tells us the rest.

Adjustments off the rule of thumb:

- **Height outliers**: very short or very tall clients move ±100–200 kcal from the base
- **Weight outliers**: well above or below the bracket — scale linearly (heavier = more, lighter = less)
- **Activity / steps**: desk job + low steps = lower start; tradie or active job = push 100–300 kcal up
- **Training frequency**: 5+ sessions/wk = nudge up; 3 sessions/wk = nudge down
- **Goal**: fat loss starts here; recomp/maintenance adds ~10–15%; lean bulk adds 200–500 kcal carb-led

**When to use a calculator vs the rule of thumb**

The Starting Macro Calculator (Tools → Calculators) is a useful sanity check, especially for outliers. The rule of thumb is faster and almost always close enough for in-the-bracket clients. Use the calculator when something feels off — a very tall or short client, an unusual training frequency, a very light or heavy bodyweight — and let it confirm or correct your starting numbers before you write the plan.

Use the rule of thumb when:
- The client lands inside the standard weight/height bracket
- Their job and activity are average
- Their training frequency is 3–5 sessions/wk
- You've coached this archetype before

Use the calculator when:
- Significantly above or below the bracket (a 110 kg male, a 45 kg female)
- Very high or very low daily activity (delivery driver, bedridden recovery client)
- A history of long deficits or post-cut maintenance — the body's TDEE is suppressed and the calculator's suppressed-output adjustment matters
- You're new to the company and want a second opinion on the number

A coaching truth: the calculator is a *guide*, not an oracle. Two calculators will disagree by 200 kcal. Pick a number, get it in front of the client, and let the data correct it. Don't get stuck running calculators in a loop — pick, deploy, observe.

**Training day vs rest day — when to introduce it**

Almost every DPperformance plan eventually runs two daily targets: a training day (TD) and a rest day (RD). The split exists because energy needs genuinely differ between training and non-training days, and because the gap becomes a useful fat-loss lever once it's in place. **But it doesn't ship on day one.**

The default ramp:

- **Day one — single calorie target.** Ship the starting number as one daily figure. Simpler for the client to absorb in week one. Less to track, less to mess up.
- **Check-in 1 — sometimes.** If the client started a touch high or progress reads slow already, introduce TD/RD here. If the client is on track, leave it.
- **Check-in 2 — almost always.** By the second check-in, most clients have TD/RD in place. The exception is the client who's already losing well at the single target. If results are good, don't add complexity. The mantra: don't make it harder if they're doing everything right and the data already shows what we need.

Standard split when it goes in:

- **Training day** = the rule-of-thumb starting number (or whatever the single target was)
- **Rest day** = ~200 kcal lower, almost entirely from carbs

Why carbs come out on rest days: training is what burns carbs. On a rest day they're not powering performance, so reducing them keeps daily protein and fat intact (preserving muscle and hormone health) while creating a real deficit. Clients sometimes find rest days slightly hungrier — predict this in the conversation when you introduce the split so it lands as expected, not as a problem.

Worked example, 80 kg target male starting cut, after TD/RD has been introduced:
- TD: 2200 kcal, ~175 g protein, ~70 g fat, ~218 g carbs
- RD: 2000 kcal, ~175 g protein, ~70 g fat, ~168 g carbs

Worked example, 58 kg target female starting cut, after TD/RD has been introduced:
- TD: 1750 kcal, ~105 g protein, ~58 g fat, ~200 g carbs
- RD: 1550 kcal, ~105 g protein, ~58 g fat, ~150 g carbs

Note: protein and fat hold across both days. Only carbs flex. This is the default once the split is live.

**The "when unsure, ask" rule**

The DPperformance rule, verbatim: *when unsure, ask.* If a client doesn't fit the bracket, has a confusing history (long Keto, recent baby, a year of under-eating), or you simply aren't certain — ask the head coach or post in the coach group before you ship. Five minutes of someone else's eyes saves a check-in's worth of recovery later. There is no penalty for asking. There is a real cost to shipping a number you don't believe in.

**What "starting calories" actually means**

A starting number is a hypothesis. The body's response over 7–14 days is the verification. We expect:

- 400 g–1 kg/wk loss in males
- 300 g–1 kg/wk loss in females (smaller females trend lower, that's normal)
- A clear downward trend across daily weights, not a single weigh-in

If we get that, the number was right. If we get more (faster loss with no extra hunger), we may have under-shot — typically fine for a few weeks, but watch performance and hunger. If we get less (flat or rising), we likely over-shot, the client's TDEE is lower than the bracket assumed, or adherence isn't where they think it is. Diagnose adherence first (Non-Calorie Stalls), then adjust.

**What this lesson sets up**

The starting number is one input. The next two lessons cover the other two: the macro split that goes inside that number (Lesson 2.2) and the deficit-pacing logic that decides how aggressive the number actually is for this specific client (Lesson 2.3). Get those three right and the plan is real. Then we hand it to the meal-structure work in Lesson 2.4 and it becomes something the client can actually live on.

lessons.title: Macronutrient Targets
lessons.summary: Protein floor, fat floor, carbs as the remainder, and how the macro split changes between training days and rest days.
lessons.body:
**Order of operations**

Once the starting calorie number is set, macros get programmed in a fixed order: **protein first, fat second, carbs as the remainder**. This order matters. Protein and fat both have biological floors below which the client suffers — muscle loss, low testosterone, hunger, recovery debt, hormonal disruption. Carbs do not have a meaningful floor at sane intakes. So we lock the floors first, then carbs absorb the remainder of the calorie budget. This is the same logic Clean Health, J3, and every credible coaching framework uses, and it's the DPperformance default.

**Protein floor: 2.2 g/kg for males, 1.8 g/kg for females (target body weight, cut phase)**

Protein is the non-negotiable. On a cut, set protein at **2.2 g/kg of target body weight for males, 1.8 g/kg for females** — meaning the weight the client is heading towards, not their current scale weight. For a 90 kg male targeting 80 kg, protein is 80 × 2.2 ≈ 175 g. For a 65 kg female targeting 58 kg, protein is 58 × 1.8 ≈ 105 g. Round to the nearest 5 g and ship.

Why these numbers, and why off target weight, not current: under a deficit, muscle retention is the single biggest threat to a transformation. The literature supports a productive range up to ~2.2 g/kg, and we sit at the top of it for males because the cost of overshooting is essentially zero (slightly more satiety, slightly more recovery support) while the cost of undershooting is real lean-mass loss. Females sit at 1.8 g/kg on a cut because their lower total calorie budget means additional protein starts to crowd out carbs and fats that matter for training performance and cycle function — but 1.8 is meaningfully above the floor of the literature, not at it. Programming off target weight (rather than current weight) prevents over-prescribing protein to a client who's holding excess fat — those calories are better spent on carbs. As the client leans down, protein intake stays where it was prescribed and naturally trends towards an even higher percentage of current weight, which is exactly what we want late in a cut.

This is a floor, not a ceiling. We're often a bit higher because protein-rich foods anchor satiety and a 5–10 g overshoot doesn't hurt anything. We're never below.

**Maintain and lean bulk: protein comes up further.** The cut numbers above are the floor when calorie space is tight. As the client moves into a maintenance phase or a lean bulk, calorie pressure releases and protein steps up:

- **Maintain**: 2.5 g/kg target body weight for males, 2.0 g/kg for females
- **Lean bulk**: up to 3.0 g/kg target body weight for males, 2.2 g/kg for females

The bulk numbers are at the top of the working range. They're not a ceiling — they're the active-growth setting. Higher protein in a surplus does three things at once: it caps the rate of fat gain (protein is the most thermic and least readily stored macro), it maintains the satiety that keeps adherence intact while calories rise, and it gives the muscle protein synthesis machinery zero excuse to slow down. The carbs and fats around it have plenty of headroom because the calorie budget is bigger; nothing is fighting for room on the plan.

Females scale up but don't push to the same multiples as males — 2.2 g/kg in a bulk is enough to serve every physiological purpose without crowding the plan, which matters more for women given the smaller absolute calorie envelope.

**Fat floor: 0.8 g/kg minimum (1 g/kg for females)**

Fat is the second floor. Set fat at **0.8 g/kg of target body weight as a minimum** for males, and **1 g/kg for females**. Below that, hormone production starts to suffer — particularly testosterone in males, and full menstrual function in females. We don't go lower. The female floor sits higher deliberately: it's the cleanest way to protect cycle function and avoid pushing the client toward the boundary, because the cost of crossing it (cycle disruption, mood, sleep, recovery) is much higher than the cost of running a slightly fatter macro split.

For an 80 kg male target, fat is at least 64 g. For a 58 kg female target, fat is at least 58 g.

Most plans run a touch above the floor — 0.9–1.0 g/kg for males, 1.0–1.2 g/kg for females — because the food preferences clients bring (eggs, avocado, peanut butter, olive oil, full-fat yogurt for some) push fat naturally to the lower-mid range. That's fine. Below the floor is where we don't go.

**Engineering fat across meal options**

Once a meal plan has 2–3 lunch/dinner alternatives, fat is no longer set per-meal — it has to land in range regardless of which option the client chooses on a given day. This is one of the easiest places for a plan to drift below floor without the coach noticing. A client who picks the leanest mince + Spud Lite + green beans option three days running can pull daily fat hundreds of grams below where it should be over a week.

The coaching move: when you build a plan, do a quick audit across every combination — pick the lowest-fat option at each meal, total it, and make sure that day still hits the floor. If it doesn't, either bump fat at a fixed meal (cooking oil, an avocado, a fixed nut butter snack) or rebuild the lower-fat option to land closer to the others. Same audit at the high end so the highest-fat combination doesn't blow protein or carb budgets either. Plans should bracket inside floor and ceiling no matter which option the client picks.

This is structural — it's a programming-time discipline, not a check-in fix. Below the floor is where we don't go.

**Carbs: whatever's left**

Once protein and fat are locked, carbs absorb the remainder of the calorie budget. There is no carb floor — sustained low-carb intakes are well-tolerated by some clients (see Lesson 2.5 for the keto and low-carb alternatives). But for the default DP system, carbs are typically the largest macro by gram count, and they live in three places: pre-workout, post-workout, and inside the main meals as rice / Spud Lite / pumpkin / sweet potato / bread.

Worked example, 80 kg target male, cut, 2200 TD kcal:
- Protein: 175 g (700 kcal) — at the male 2.2 g/kg cut floor
- Fat: 70 g (630 kcal)
- Remainder: 870 kcal → 218 g carbs

Worked example, 58 kg target female, cut, 1750 TD kcal:
- Protein: 105 g (420 kcal) — at the female 1.8 g/kg cut floor
- Fat: 58 g (522 kcal) — at the female 1.0 g/kg fat floor
- Remainder: 808 kcal → 202 g carbs

(Female numbers tend to round generously because plans on lower calories benefit from a slightly higher relative carb intake to support training output.)

**Why these floors exist — the four reasons**

You will sometimes get pushback from a client (or a curious nutrition-Twitter follower they have) on why we don't push protein higher or carbs lower. The four reasons to keep memorised:

1. **Performance.** Carbs power lifting. A client who eats their carbs trains harder, lifts more, and builds or retains more muscle. Cutting carbs to "lose faster" wrecks the gym work that's making the cut worth doing.
2. **Satiety.** Protein is the most satiating macro per calorie — by a significant margin. The cut-phase protein floor (2.2 g/kg for males, 1.8 g/kg for females) exists partly to keep hunger manageable across the day. Drop protein and the client gets hungrier on the same calories.
3. **Recovery.** Protein is the substrate for muscle protein synthesis. Below the floor, recovery slows, soreness lingers, and the next session is worse than it should be.
4. **Hormone health.** Fat below 0.8 g/kg suppresses testosterone in males and disrupts menstrual function in females. Both effects show up within weeks. Both are reversible — but we shouldn't be causing them in the first place.

**Rest day vs training day macro splits**

The standard rest-day adjustment (from Lesson 2.1) is ~200 kcal lower, almost entirely from carbs. Protein and fat hold flat. Why:

- Protein: muscle retention is a daily need, not a training-day need. We don't drop protein on rest days.
- Fat: hormones are a 24/7 process. Fat stays flat.
- Carbs: the day's lowered training demand means lower carb need. Pulling carbs gives us the rest-day deficit cleanly.

For a male client on a cut at 175 g protein / 70 g fat (80 kg target):
- TD: 2200 kcal → 218 g carbs
- RD: 2000 kcal → 168 g carbs

Same protein, same fat, ~50 g less carbs. That's the entire structure.

**What about high/low day splits?**

Once a client has been in a deficit for 3–4 weeks and we want a sharper lever, the rest-day adjustment can grow into a full high-day / low-day split (e.g., 5 high / 2 low, then 4 high / 3 low). This is Lever 3 in the Cutting Decision Tree — covered in Module 5. For now: training day vs rest day is the starting structure for every plan. Anything beyond that is a later adjustment, not a starting point.

**Common new-coach mistakes**

Three patterns to avoid in the first 8 weeks of coaching:

- **Setting protein off current weight on a high-BF client.** A 110 kg male at 2.2 g/kg current = 242 g protein, which crowds out carbs and makes the plan harder to live on. Use target weight.
- **Cutting fat below the floor to "save calories" on small females.** Female plans on 1500 TD kcal can feel calorie-tight, and it's tempting to drop fat to 35–40 g. Don't — hormones suffer first, then adherence goes. Cut a snack or rebalance carbs instead.
- **Letting carbs disappear on cuts.** Aggressive coaches cut carbs hard "to drop water" — clients then under-perform in the gym, lose muscle, and stall. Carbs are not the enemy of fat loss. Calories are.

Macros are not where the magic happens. The magic is calorie balance over weeks, executed with adherence. Macros exist to make sure that calorie balance lands on muscle, hormone, and performance correctly — not on the scale alone.

lessons.title: Deficit Pacing — Graduated by Body Fat
lessons.summary: Why a single "1 kg/wk cap" is wrong, the body-fat thresholds for aggressive vs conservative pacing, and the lean-client trap.
lessons.body:
**Why one rate doesn't fit every client**

A 32% body-fat male and a 12% body-fat male are different physiological systems. The high-BF client has large fat stores, often elevated leptin and insulin, and can mobilise body fat at a high rate without losing muscle. The lean client has low leptin, sensitised hunger, and any aggressive deficit comes straight off muscle and performance. Capping both at the same "1 kg/wk maximum" is leaving fat loss on the table for one and risking muscle loss on the other.

DPperformance pacing is graduated by body fat. Higher BF clients can run faster in the early phase of a cut. Lean clients run slower, on the conservative DP rate, all the way through. As any client leans out, their personal rate tapers from wherever it started down to the conservative rate by the time they're inside their lean-zone.

**The body-fat thresholds**

These are working thresholds — not bright lines, but useful brackets:

- **>25–30% body fat (males) / >30–35% (females)** — high-BF zone. Aggressive deficit appropriate. Targeted rate: **1.2–1.5 kg/wk** in the first 4–6 weeks.
- **15–25% males / 22–30% females** — standard zone. Targeted rate: **0.8–1.0 kg/wk**, scaling down as they lean.
- **12–15% males / 18–22% females** — late-cut zone. Targeted rate: **0.5–0.8 kg/wk**.
- **<12% males / <18% females** — lean zone. Targeted rate: **conservative DP rate (0.3–0.5 kg/wk maximum)**. Past this point, faster comes off muscle and lifts, full stop.

These are weekly *averages*, not single-week reads. A 1.6 kg drop on the scale in a single week with carbs cut is not a 1.6 kg fat-loss week — most of it is glycogen and water. Always read across 2–3 weeks of data before adjusting.

**Why a high-BF client can — and should — run more aggressive**

The reasoning is physiological. Higher body fat = larger leptin pool, more insulin signal, and a much larger fat-mass buffer. The body has more energy on tap and isn't fighting the deficit the way a lean body does. A 1.5 kg/wk loss in a 32% BF male is roughly 1% of body weight — well inside the literature's safe range for muscle retention.

A separate practical reason: **early visible results drive adherence**. A client who loses 6 kg in the first 4 weeks is locked in. A client who loses 1.5 kg in 4 weeks is wondering whether the program works. For high-BF clients especially, the early aggressive phase pays off across the whole block in compliance.

This is a deliberate departure from a one-size cap. The Clean Health and J3 evidence both support it. Daniel built the position around exactly these data points.

**The 1% bw/wk rule and the lean-client trap**

The single most-cited number in the muscle-retention literature is **>1% bodyweight per week loss = real muscle and performance cost**. Garthe (2011) showed faster losses (>1% bw/wk) preserved less lean mass than slower losses; Mero (2010) and Hulmi (2017) reach similar conclusions in lean populations.

For an 80 kg client, 1% = 800 g/wk. For a 60 kg client, 1% = 600 g/wk. So the same "1 kg/wk" target is **inside the safe zone for an 80 kg client and outside it for a 60 kg client**. This is why we don't run a single rate. The graduated approach uses % bw thresholds in disguise — the lean-zone cap of 0.3–0.5 kg/wk for a 65 kg client is well under 1% bw, and that's the point.

The lean-client trap: late in a cut, clients who are visually leaner often *demand* faster loss because they can see the finish line. Their adherence is high, their hunger is low, "let's just push through." Push past 1% bw/wk in this window and you're trading fat for muscle and gym performance. The right move is the wizard principle — predict the slowdown, name it as the goal, and hold the line.

> "We're at the lean part of the cut now. The rate's going to slow down — that's exactly what we want. Faster from here just costs us muscle and gym progress, and we've worked too hard for that. Last 4 weeks we trade speed for keeping everything we've built."

**Tapering as the client leans out**

Inside a single block, the rate should taper. A high-BF male who started at 1.5 kg/wk should be at 0.8–1.0 kg/wk by week 4–6 and at 0.5–0.8 kg/wk by week 8–10 if the cut runs that long. The taper isn't an adjustment we make — it's an adjustment we expect. The body produces it naturally as adaptive thermogenesis kicks in and fat stores reduce. If a client *doesn't* taper and is still losing 1.5 kg/wk at 12% BF, something is wrong (under-eating, over-cardio, lying about food, illness) and you investigate.

**Females vs males pacing nuance**

Three differences that change the practical pacing:

1. **Lower starting weight.** Most female clients are 55–75 kg. The same kg/wk target is a bigger % of bodyweight. We use slightly lower kg/wk targets for that reason — not because females respond worse, but because the % is what matters.
2. **Cycle masking.** 2–3 weeks of apparent stall around the menstrual cycle is normal water retention, not stalled loss. Compare same-cycle-phase weights (covered as item 6 in the non-calorie stalls list — Module 5 Lesson 5.4). Don't pull levers on a cycle-masked week.
3. **Lower lean-zone threshold.** 18% BF in a female is roughly the equivalent of 12% BF in a male in terms of essential fat and hormonal threshold. The conservative rate kicks in earlier on the BF scale for females.

**Block length: symptom-driven, not calendar-driven**

Pacing is a within-block question. Block length is its own decision — and we don't impose a fixed week ceiling. A 14-week cut on a client who is sleeping well, training strong, and adherent is a 14-week cut. The trigger to step out is symptoms, not the calendar: persistent sleep degradation, mood drops, training performance regressing, adherence visibly cracking, or the client genuinely fatigued in a way that has accumulated across multiple weeks. Lesson 2.6 and Module 5 cover the diet-break mechanics in detail.

**The exception that *does* warrant scheduled breaks** is the very long cut — clients targeting 20 kg+ of total loss. The cumulative metabolic and adherence load on a 6-month-plus deficit is genuinely high, and these clients benefit from planned diet breaks at sensible intervals (every 8–10 kg of loss, or every 3–4 months in continuous deficit) regardless of week-to-week symptoms. That's planning, not gatekeeping — it makes the back half of the cut achievable.

**The decision a coach actually makes**

For each new client, the pacing decision is one question: **what's their starting body fat, and what's the target rate for that bracket?** Once you've answered that, you've calibrated the deficit size, the calorie target, and what "good progress" looks like. You're going to see the answer in scale data, photos, and gym performance over the first 2–3 weeks. Adjust off that — not off a single weigh-in, not off the client's mood, and not off what worked for the last client. Pacing is per-physiology.

**The shorthand**

- High BF: push hard, expect 1.2–1.5 kg/wk early, taper as they lean
- Standard: 0.8–1.0 kg/wk, tapering through the block
- Lean: conservative 0.3–0.5 kg/wk, never above 1% bw/wk
- Block length: no fixed cap; step out on symptoms, plan breaks for cuts targeting 20kg+
- Read 2–3 weeks of data, not single weigh-ins
- Female pacing uses lower kg/wk targets and respects cycle masking

lessons.title: Plan Structure — The 3+2 Meal Model
lessons.summary: The default DP meal-structured plan, brand-spec rules, the meal-simplicity formula, the macros exception, and the approved food list.
lessons.body:
**The default plan**

Every DPperformance client receives a structured meal plan. The default shape is **3 main meals + 2 snacks (pre-workout + post-workout)**. This isn't graduated to flexibility for "experienced" clients — every client gets a structured plan, regardless of how long they've been training or tracking. The reason isn't paternalism. It's adherence math.

**Why structure beats IIFYM as the default**

Decision fatigue is the single quiet killer of long-term plans. A client tracking macros decides what to eat 4–6 times a day. By Friday afternoon, after a stressful work week, they're making a tired food decision while opening the fridge — and that's where the plan loses 200–500 kcal of accidental excess. They didn't fail discipline. They ran out of decision capacity.

A structured meal plan removes those decisions. The client knows their breakfast. They know their lunch. They know what's in the post-workout shake. They walk into the kitchen on autopilot and the plan executes itself. Adherence is dramatically higher because the friction is dramatically lower.

There's also the experience side. Clients pay for an answer, not a calorie budget. "Here's exactly what to eat" is a clearer product than "here's 2200 kcal — figure it out." The first one feels like coaching. The second one feels like homework.

**The 3+2 default structure**

The shape every plan starts as:

- **Breakfast** — 1 option to start (sweet or savoury)
- **Lunch** — 1–2 options
- **Dinner** — 1–2 options (often interchangeable with lunch)
- **Pre-workout** — fast-digesting carbs, low fat (rice cakes + honey, banana, LCM bar)
- **Post-workout** — high protein, easy to digest (whey + water, yogurt + whey)

Total of about 5 meals across the day. Pre and post are scaled to training-day calories — they typically come out or shrink on rest days, which is one of the cleanest ways to create the rest-day deficit (Lesson 2.1).

**The meal simplicity rule**

Each main meal follows the formula: **1 protein + 1 carb + veg/filler + optional fat**. That's it.

Worked examples:
- Chicken breast + jasmine rice + green beans + olive oil
- 5% lean beef mince + Spud Lite potato + pumpkin + olive oil
- Steak + sweet potato + spinach + a small olive oil drizzle

This formula exists because it makes everything downstream easier: macro adjustments, food swaps, eating-out choices, travel options, the whole machine. When a meal has six different ingredients with overlapping macros, adjusting it is a pain. When a meal has four clean components, the coach can swap any one of them without rebuilding the plan.

**Brand specification — adapt to client region**

Default templates use Australian brands because Daniel built the system on what was on his shelf. Coaches must adapt to client region. Ask the client during onboarding which brands they actually use for: high-protein yogurt, cereal, bread or wraps, protein bars, rice products. Specify the brand in the plan when macros vary across products or accuracy matters.

The Aussie defaults (always swap to local equivalents):
- **Yogurt:** YoPro, Chobani low-fat Greek
- **Cereal:** Carman's Natural Bircher Muesli, XO Crunch, Weetbix
- **Rice products:** Ceres brown rice cakes, Good Food Society cream of rice
- **Potato:** Spud Lite (low-cal high-volume potato — hero food in cuts)
- **Protein bars:** Cold Press fibre-boost bars

US client without YoPro? Sub Oikos Pro or Two Good. UK client without Carman's? Sub Lizi's. Local equivalent matters more than the exact brand — the rule is the macro accuracy, not the loyalty.

**The DP approved food list**

The canonical list. Memorise these — they're the Lego pieces every plan is built from.

**Proteins** — chicken breast, 5% lean beef mince, kangaroo mince, chicken/pork mince, eye fillet, porterhouse, rump, tuna (spring water), whey isolate, vegan protein, eggs / egg whites, high-protein yogurt.

**Carbohydrates** — jasmine rice, potato, Spud Lite, sweet potato, pumpkin, couscous, quinoa, sourdough, bagel, English muffin, Carman's Bircher, XO Crunch, Weetbix, Ceres rice cakes, Good Food Society cream of rice. Fruits: banana, raspberries, blueberries, strawberries, orange, pineapple. Fast carbs: honey, jam.

**Fats** — olive oil, sesame oil, butter (cooking); eggs, avocado, peanut butter, almond butter, cashew butter, chia seeds (whole-food fats).

**Fillers / low-cal veg** — spinach, leafy greens, green beans, tomatoes, carrots, eggplant, peas, pumpkin, cabbage, crushed canned tomatoes.

**Gut support** — psyllium husk, kefir, sauerkraut.

**Convenience / lifestyle additions** — protein bars (Cold Press or local equivalent), pre-made meals (Papa Macros / MMC or local equivalent). Use for time-poor clients or low cooking adherence.

The principle behind the list: **physique foods over "healthy foods."** Granola is "healthy" and quietly puts a 200 g serving at 800 kcal. Spud Lite is a physique food — 60 kcal per 100 g, fills the plate, hits the deficit. We program for body composition, not for whatever the latest wellness trend looks like.

**The macros exception**

If a client specifically asks to track macros instead of following a meal plan, we allow it — but the deal is conditional:

- They hit the macro target
- They show us the logs (every check-in, no exceptions)
- We monitor results

If progress stalls, our first move is to gently steer them back to a meal plan. We know decision fatigue is usually the cause. Script:

> "I think the macros are getting a bit fuzzy — happens to everyone after a few weeks. Let's flip back to a structured plan for the next 3 weeks and see if things tighten up. We can revisit macros after."

If after that conversation they still want to run macros, we respect their autonomy and let them. We don't argue people into a system they don't want — we just stay accountable for the result and keep the door open to swap back if it's not working.

This is the autonomy principle. Coach hard for the system that gets the result, but don't strong-arm a client into it.

**The "5+ alternatives" rule**

If a meal in someone's plan accumulates 5 or more alternatives over time, ask: *which are you actually using? Which can I delete?* Cluttered plans look generous but feel overwhelming. A clean plan with 2–3 working options per meal beats a 7-option plan the client never reads. Prune regularly.

**What this lesson sets up**

Plan structure is the spine of the work. The next lesson covers what to do when this default doesn't fit a particular client — keto, vegan, IF, Mediterranean. Lesson 2.6 covers what happens when the structured plan meets a wedding, a holiday, or a Friday night out.

lessons.title: Multi-System Fluency — Beyond the Default
lessons.summary: When to deviate from the DP default to keto, IF, vegan, Mediterranean, low-carb, paleo, or isocaloric — and how each one fits.
lessons.body:
**The default and the alternatives**

The DP default is a moderate-carb, high-protein, animal-protein-anchored, structured 3+2 plan built on Aussie staples. It works for the majority of clients because it's been engineered for adherence in a busy life. But "majority" is not "all." Religion, ethics, culture, gut health, training context, and personal preference all produce clients for whom the default isn't the right fit — and forcing them into it is how we lose them.

Multi-system fluency means knowing the alternatives well enough to deploy them when the default genuinely doesn't suit. It does **not** mean offering every client a menu of options on day one. The default is the default for a reason. Alternatives exist for genuine fit — not for novelty, not for trend chasing, not because the client read something on Instagram last week.

**The trigger: genuine fit**

Deviate from the default when one of the following is true:

- **Religious or cultural requirement** (halal, kosher, vegetarian/vegan by belief, Ramadan)
- **Ethical commitment** (vegan, vegetarian, sustainability-driven)
- **Medical or biological reason** (severe IBS responding to FODMAP, diagnosed insulin resistance, allergies)
- **Long-standing eating pattern that already works** (a client who has eaten IF-style for 5 years and lifts well — don't break what works)
- **Lifestyle constraint that makes the default impractical** (a shift worker for whom 3 main meals on a diurnal schedule is impossible)

Deviate when at least one of these applies. Don't deviate when the trigger is "I'm bored" — that's a swap-library problem inside the default, not a system change.

**The default DP system — characteristics**

The system you're already coaching, named explicitly so you can compare:

- Moderate carb (typically 35–50% of calories), high protein (cut floor 2.2 g/kg male / 1.8 g/kg female; rising in maintain and bulk), moderate fat (0.8 g/kg male / 1.0 g/kg female floor)
- Animal-protein anchored (chicken, beef, eggs, yogurt, whey)
- Structured 3+2 meals
- TD/RD calorie split with carb cycling
- Aussie staples (or regional equivalents)
- Whole-food default with named convenience options

**Alternative 1 — Keto**

Carbs <50 g/day, fat 60–75% of calories, moderate protein. Body shifts to fat-and-ketone fuel.

When it works: clients who genuinely feel better low-carb (rare but real), clients with a long stable history of low-carb eating, clients with severe insulin sensitivity issues confirmed by their doctor.

When it doesn't: most lifters. Glycogen-depleted lifting underperforms — strength drops, pumps disappear, recovery slows. The first 2 weeks of keto include "keto flu" that nobody warns clients about. Adherence in social contexts is hard (carbs are everywhere).

What to watch for: low energy in training, brain fog past week 2 (should resolve), constipation (fibre intake collapses without grains/fruit), low electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium). If gym performance crashes and stays crashed past week 4, the system isn't fitting and you should pull back.

**Alternative 2 — Intermittent fasting (IF)**

Eating compressed to a window — typically 8 hours (e.g., 12pm–8pm). Total calories unchanged.

When it works: clients with a strong morning aversion to food, shift workers whose schedule makes morning eating impractical, clients who already do this naturally and just want it formalised.

When it doesn't: clients training fasted who can't hit pre-workout fuel, clients who consistently overeat in the window because hunger compounds, clients with a history of disordered eating (the restriction frame is risky — handle with care).

What to watch for: under-eating (the window can collapse a 2200 kcal target to 1700 by accident), training-day energy if pre-workout is squeezed out, irritability in the first 2 weeks. Keep protein at the same total — don't let IF erode the protein floor.

**Alternative 3 — Vegan**

All animal products excluded. Protein from legumes, tofu, tempeh, seitan, vegan protein powders, soy, lentils, beans.

When it works: clients with a genuine ethical commitment. Don't fight this — adherence will be perfect because the value is intrinsic.

When it doesn't: when a client says "I want to try going vegan" with no underlying commitment. Vegan plans are work — protein is harder to hit, satiety is lower per gram, and the food list is genuinely smaller. We wouldn't put a client there voluntarily.

What to watch for: hitting the protein floor (often need vegan protein powder daily, sometimes twice), B12 supplementation (mandatory for true vegans), iron and zinc adequacy. Plan templates need rebuilding from scratch — don't just remove animal proteins from the default and call it vegan.

**Alternative 4 — Mediterranean**

Olive oil, fish, seafood, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, moderate dairy, low red meat, low processed food.

When it works: clients with cardiovascular concerns, clients who genuinely prefer this food culture, older clients (the literature is strong on long-term health markers).

When it doesn't: it's not really an "alternative" so much as a flavoured default — and flavour matters, but the macros and structure look very similar to the DP default. Often the right move is to keep the structure and re-skin the food list.

What to watch for: fat creep (olive oil is generous), expensive food (good fish costs money), it can shade towards under-protein if grains crowd out animal protein.

**Alternative 5 — Isocaloric (consistent every day)**

Same calories every day, no TD/RD split, no high/low days.

When it works: clients who hate variability, clients early in their tracking journey who can't yet read a more complex split, very-busy clients who want one number.

When it doesn't: clients in late deficit phases where the TD/RD split is the lever creating the deficit, clients with a clear training/rest day energy gap.

What to watch for: this is more "default minus the carb cycle" than a new system. Often a transitional setup, not a forever one.

**Alternative 6 — Low-carb (not keto)**

Carbs 100–150 g/day. Moderate fat, high protein. Closer to the default than keto but with a clear directional lean.

When it works: clients who report better energy and lower hunger on lower carbs (some genuinely do), clients with mild insulin-sensitivity flags, clients training 2–3 times a week (lower training demand = lower carb need).

When it doesn't: clients training 5+ days a week pushing volume — they'll under-recover. High-BF clients in early aggressive deficit need the carbs for performance.

What to watch for: gym performance, sleep quality, mood. Same flags as keto, dialled down.

**Alternative 7 — Paleo**

No grains, no legumes, no dairy, no processed food. Whole-food meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit, nuts.

When it works: clients with genuine grain or legume intolerances, clients who already eat this way and want it formalised.

When it doesn't: hitting protein and carbs efficiently is harder without grains and dairy. Spud Lite and pumpkin work; rice and oats don't.

What to watch for: carb intake creeping low by accident, grocery bill (grass-fed meat is expensive), social eating (paleo at restaurants is doable but limiting).

**The "don't force the client into the system" principle**

The system serves the client — never the reverse. If the default is a poor fit, swap. If an alternative becomes a poor fit, swap again. Coaches who get attached to a system they like start losing clients who don't fit it. Stay loose.

The flag for success is the same regardless of system: weekly progress in the right direction, sustainable adherence, training output preserved, hunger manageable, mood stable. If those five hold, the system is working. If two or more fail, change the system.

**The default lives at the centre**

Knowing the alternatives well makes you a better coach for the default, because you understand what trade-off each alternative is making and why the default sits in its specific spot. The default isn't arbitrary — it's the system that maximises adherence for a generic busy professional. Every alternative is a deliberate departure for a specific reason. Use that lens.

lessons.title: Off-Plan Meals, Alcohol & Social Events
lessons.summary: How to coach the meals out and nights out so they fit inside the week — and how to read and respond to the inevitable scale spikes.
lessons.body:
**The lifestyle frame**

DPperformance clients have lives. They have weddings, work dinners, a friend's 30th, a Friday night out, a Sunday lunch with the parents. These are normal and expected. Our job is not to ask them to refuse — that's not lifestyle coaching, that's contest prep. Our job is to make those events fit inside the week without erasing the deficit.

If a client thinks the program means saying no to dinner with their partner, they're wrong about the program. Coach them toward "yes, and here's how" — that's the product they're paying for.

**The off-plan meal day template**

The principle: bank calories earlier in the day so the evening meal fits. The protein and the structure stay. The padding around the meal goes.

The DP template:

1. Remove carbs and fats from breakfast and lunch (e.g., muesli → just yogurt; chicken/rice/veg → chicken + veg)
2. Remove carb snacks (pre-workout snacks) — even if training that day
3. Keep mostly lean protein foods through the day
4. Dinner = the off-plan meal, eaten without tracking

This produces a day that hits protein, sits at high satiety from the protein-and-veg load, and runs 600–800 kcal lower than rest day for females and 800–1200 kcal lower for males before the off-plan dinner. That gap is the buffer that absorbs the dinner.

Worked example — average male, off-plan day:
- Breakfast: yogurt + whey only (skip the muesli + honey + nut butter)
- Lunch: chicken + green beans + a small olive oil drizzle (skip the rice + pumpkin)
- No pre-workout snack
- Train (or don't)
- Dinner: the meal out, eaten without tracking
- Skip post-workout if late evening

Calories pre-dinner: ~700 kcal. Day's protein already at ~120 g. Hunger is manageable because protein is high. Client walks into dinner with a real budget to use.

**The wizard predict — frame this on the welcome video**

Set the off-plan meal frame *before* the first one happens. The script:

> "When you've got a dinner out coming up, just let me know — I'll send you the off-plan day template. You'll eat lighter through the day so you can enjoy the meal at night. The week stays on track and you don't have to pick between the program and your social life."

When the client uses it for the first time and it works, the relationship just got stronger. The wizard principle in action.

**Restaurant guidelines**

When the client is choosing what to order, the priority list:

- **Protein-led:** steak, chicken, grilled fish, lamb chops. Aim for a fist of protein on the plate.
- **Avoid pure carb+fat:** cheese pizza, arancini, fried starters, creamy pasta. These are the calorie-dense traps with little protein anchor.
- **Vegetables on the side, not creamed:** salad, grilled veg, side of greens.
- **Limit fried:** chips, deep-fried starters, anything battered.

For a highly adherent client running a sharp cut: they can ask the restaurant to cook the protein with minimal oil/butter — most restaurants will do this without fuss. We don't make every client do this. We do offer it for clients pushing for a leaner finish.

For frequent eaters-out: coach the heuristic. They should be able to walk into any restaurant and pick a protein-anchored meal in 30 seconds.

**Alcohol — the post-drinking spillover is the real risk**

Alcohol itself rarely wrecks a cut. Five drinks is ~500 kcal — annoying, not catastrophic. The real damage is what happens *around* the drinks: the late-night fast food, the next-day greasy breakfast, the "rest day" that became a 4000 kcal rest day.

Five drinks (500 kcal) → late-night burger run (1200 kcal) → next-day full English breakfast (1500 kcal) → afternoon hangover snack (500 kcal). That's 3700 kcal of spillover on top of the actual drinks. That's the deficit erased for the entire week.

Drink choices that minimise calorie damage:
- Vodka soda, tequila soda — ~80–100 kcal per drink
- Spirits with diet mixers — same range
- Shots — short, fast, low calorie

Avoid: cocktails (often 300–400 kcal each), beer (~150 kcal each, drunk in volume), creamy drinks, sugary mixers.

Before the night: bank calories during the day (modified off-plan template), eat protein before drinking (slows absorption, anchors satiety), encourage enjoyment without restriction once the night starts.

The critical coaching message — say it before every event:

> "The drinks themselves are fine. The thing to watch is what happens after — the late-night food and the next day. Get straight back on plan tomorrow morning, no compensating, no skipping breakfast. The drinks are not the problem; the spillover is."

**The post-event coaching rule**

After a night out or a meal out: **return directly to plan**. Don't compensate. Don't slash calories. Don't add cardio. Don't skip meals.

The reasoning is twofold. First, compensating reinforces the binge/restrict cycle, which is the actual disordered-eating pattern we want to keep clients out of. Second, the scale spike from a single off-plan meal is water, sodium, glycogen, and gut content — not fat. Pulling levers to "fix" water with food restriction creates a real deficit on top of the recovery, which makes the client miserable for no benefit.

The script:

> "Don't try to undo it. Just go back to plan today — same breakfast, same lunch, same training. The scale will be up for 2–3 days because of water and salt — that's not fat, that's just the body resetting. By Wednesday/Thursday it'll drop back through the trend line."

**Why scale spikes after social meals**

Memorise this list — it's the client-education tool you'll use weekly:

- **Carbs → glycogen + water.** Each gram of glycogen binds ~3 g of water. A high-carb dinner can add 1–2 kg of glycogen-bound water inside 24 hours.
- **Sodium → water retention.** Restaurant food is salt-dense. Sodium pulls water into the body's compartments. 3–5 days for it to normalise.
- **Sugar → water retention.** Same mechanism, faster onset.
- **Gut content volume.** Large meals genuinely sit in the gut for 24–36 hours. That's mass on the scale.
- **Alcohol → dehydration → rebound retention.** The body over-corrects after alcohol, retaining water for 1–2 days.
- **Poor sleep → cortisol → water retention.** Late nights elevate cortisol and aldosterone, which causes sodium and water retention.

None of these are fat. Fat doesn't move that fast. A 1.5 kg overnight scale rise is physically impossible to be fat — that would require ~13,500 kcal of surplus in one meal, which no human eats.

**Recognising unreported off-plan meals from the data**

Sometimes a client doesn't report an off-plan meal — they're either embarrassed, didn't want to "make a thing of it," or thought it was too small to mention. Patterns to watch for:

- Single high weigh-in on Friday/Saturday/Sunday that doesn't match their reported intake
- Sudden 1–1.5 kg spike followed by a steady drop over 3 days
- "Stalled" weeks where the average is masked by one big spike
- Mood shift in the check-in narrative ("a bit off track" without specifics)

When you see this, name it warmly and non-judgementally:

> "Looks like you might have had a meal out or a social event around Friday — totally fine, hope it was a good one. The spike you're seeing is just water and salt, not fat. Let's just stay on plan and it'll drop back through the week."

This signals: I see what's happening, I'm not angry, here's what it actually means, here's what you do next. Three weeks of that kind of response and the client starts reporting events upfront, because the relationship is safe.

**The TL;DR coach summary**

- Meals out are normal, expected, plannable
- Bank calories earlier in the day (off-plan template)
- Order protein-led at restaurants
- The drinks aren't the problem — the spillover is
- Return to plan after, never compensate
- A scale spike post-event is water, not fat — and you have the script to prove it

Coached well, off-plan meals are a feature of the program, not a bug. Coached badly, they're where retention quietly leaks. Treat every event as a coaching moment.
