lessons.title: Hypertrophy Fundamentals
lessons.summary: Mechanical tension as the primary driver, progressive overload as the DP standard, the Dynamic Double Progression rule, and why hypertrophy programming applies to every client.
lessons.body:
**Why hypertrophy is the engine for every client**

Every DPperformance client trains for hypertrophy. Not powerlifting, not CrossFit, not "general fitness" — hypertrophy. That's true for a 42-year-old mum looking to lose 8 kg, a 28-year-old tradie wanting to put on size, a 55-year-old executive who hasn't trained in a decade, and an experienced lifter chasing the next 3 kg of muscle. The mechanism is the same in every body, the prescription scales by experience and physiology, and the visible result — the thing the client actually paid for — comes from the same lever.

Lifestyle-first does not mean training-light. The transformations we put up are built on real, structured hypertrophy work. Coaches who under-train clients because "they're a busy professional" are leaving the actual product on the table. The client doesn't pay us to keep them in the gym for an hour a week — they pay us to change their body.

**Mechanical tension is the primary mechanism**

The current best understanding of hypertrophy converges on one mechanism above the rest: **mechanical tension**. Hard, controlled muscular contractions against meaningful resistance — taken close to failure — drive the signalling cascade that builds muscle. Metabolic stress and muscle damage exist as supporting factors, but they're downstream. Tension is the lever.

Practically, that means:

- Every working set should produce real mechanical tension on the target muscle
- Effort matters more than fancy variations
- Range of motion through the muscle's stretched position is non-negotiable
- Tempo control on the eccentric (the lowering phase) is where a lot of the tension lives
- Cheating reps with momentum, partial range, or off-target compensations costs you the actual stimulus

A client doing 10 reps of bicep curls with a 12 kg dumbbell using strict form is producing real tension. The same client doing 10 reps with 16 kg using shoulder swing and bouncing the bottom is doing a different, worse exercise — and getting less hypertrophy out of it. Form is not pedantic. Form is the dose.

**Progressive overload — the DP standard**

If tension is the mechanism, **progressive overload** is the way you keep producing it across weeks and months. The body adapts to a stimulus quickly. The same weight for the same reps next week is not the same stimulus — it's an easier stimulus, and the muscle won't grow.

The DPperformance standard for progressive overload, written so a coach can quote it cold:

- **Same weight + 1 more rep** than last session = progress
- **Same reps + 2.5 kg more weight** than last session = progress
- **Either of those, on the same exercise, week-over-week** = the block is working

That's it. Not a complicated periodisation table, not undulating microcycles — a simple rule the client can hold in their head and the coach can verify from the log. **Adding even one rep is real progress.** Clients sometimes wait for a "big jump" before logging a win — coach them out of that. One rep is the unit, and one rep a week, compounded across an 8-week block, is genuinely transformative.

When a client beats both numbers in the same session — hits the top of their rep range *and* uses a heavier load — that's an exceptional session, but the rule still holds: pick which lever moves next session. We don't double-progress and double-progress until something breaks.

**Dynamic Double Progression — the autoregulated rule**

The mechanism for executing progressive overload in DP plans is the **Dynamic Double Progression (DDP)** model, lifted from the J3 framework Daniel uses with senior clients. It's the cleanest, most client-proof way to keep load and reps moving together.

The DDP rule, in plain language:

- Each exercise is prescribed with a **rep range**, not a single rep target (e.g. 8–12 reps)
- The client picks a load they can hit *somewhere inside* the range with the prescribed effort
- **If they exceed the top of the range** (e.g. they get 13 on a 12-rep cap) — increase the weight next session by the smallest increment available (typically 2.5 kg)
- **If they fall short of the bottom by 3 or more reps** (e.g. they get 5 on an 8–12 set) — pull the weight back slightly and rebuild
- **If they're inside the range** — same weight next session, push for one more rep

That's the autoregulation. The client isn't waiting for the coach to tell them what to lift — they're climbing the rep range, then jumping the weight, then climbing the new range again. The coach reads the log and confirms the trajectory.

DDP is robust to a bad day. If a client gets sick mid-block and their next session is a rep short, they don't deload — they just hold the weight and try again next week. Adherence is the only thing that breaks DDP. Even slow progression on a few exercises beats no progression on all of them.

**Why hypertrophy applies to every client (yes, every one)**

Two questions come up constantly from new clients and new coaches:

*"I'm cutting — should I switch to high-rep, light-weight 'toning' work?"* No. The single biggest mistake clients make on a cut is dropping training intensity. The hypertrophy stimulus *is* the muscle-retention signal. Dropping load and reps is what tells the body "you don't need this muscle anymore" — exactly the opposite of what we want. We hold the training stimulus and let the deficit do the fat-loss work. The muscle stays because we kept telling it to.

*"I'm a woman — should I be doing cardio-style training instead of lifting?"* No. Female clients respond to the same mechanism — mechanical tension, progressive overload — and respond very well to it. The prescription is genuinely different from a male client (Lesson 3.5 covers it in full), but the engine is identical. Light-and-toned is a marketing fiction; visible glute and posterior development comes from progressive overload on hard hinging, squatting, and pulling work.

The two correct answers, said warmly:

> "Cut or build, the training stays the same. The food creates the body composition change — the training keeps the muscle there for it to land on."

> "Heavy training is what builds the shape you actually want. The cardio side keeps energy expenditure up, but the lifting is what changes the body."

**Reassessment cadence — week 4 of a block**

A block is typically 8–10 weeks (Lesson 3.6 covers mesocycle structure). The internal checkpoint is **week 4**. At week 4, you read the log:

- Are the working weights moving up week-over-week?
- Are the rep counts climbing inside the prescribed range?
- Are there exercises stuck at the same numbers for 3+ weeks?

If the trajectory is clean, the block runs to completion. If two or more exercises have stalled, something needs adjusting *inside* the current block — usually a small load reset (back off 2.5 kg, climb the rep range cleanly), occasionally an effort recalibration (the client is leaving more in the tank than they think — Lesson 3.2). Don't change the whole block at week 4. Diagnose specifically and adjust narrowly.

**The frame to carry forward**

The job for the rest of this module: take the simple mechanism (tension), the simple progression rule (DDP, +1 rep or +2.5 kg), and build a real, structured plan around them. Effort, volume, exercise selection, splits, female adjustments, and mesocycle structure are all decisions made in service of producing tension week after week. Don't lose the mechanism in the complexity. Tension. Progression. Adherence. Repeat.

lessons.title: Effort — 0–1 RIR With Capped Volume
lessons.summary: The DP working-set effort standard, the volume tradeoff, perceived vs true failure, and how to coach effort so the client actually delivers it.
lessons.body:
**The DP standard, stated clearly**

Working sets in a DPperformance plan run at **0–1 RIR**. RIR — Reps In Reserve — is how many more reps the client could have done with good form before genuine failure. 0 RIR means the next rep would not have happened with clean technique. 1 RIR means one more was technically there.

The split by lift type:

- **Compound lifts** (squat, deadlift, bench, row, overhead press, hip thrust) — **0–1 RIR** on the working set, leaning toward 1 most weeks. Compounds carry more systemic fatigue, so we keep one rep in reserve to protect recovery for the rest of the session and the rest of the week.
- **Isolation and machine work** (curls, extensions, lateral raises, leg curls, leg extensions, cable work) — **0 RIR**. Push to the point where the next rep does not happen with good form. The fatigue cost of true failure on an isolation is small; the stimulus payoff is large.

That's the whole rule. Coaches who try to coach a single number across the whole program (everything at 0 RIR, or everything at 2 RIR) miss what each lift type actually needs.

**Why true failure on every set isn't sustainable — the volume tradeoff**

There's a real-world tradeoff that shapes every program: **the harder you train, the fewer sets you can recover from.** A client doing 6 sets per muscle group at 0 RIR with full effort is producing more total stimulus per set, but they cannot recover from 6 such sets the way they could from 6 sets at 3 RIR.

This is the universal tradeoff in hypertrophy programming:

- **Higher RIR (more reps in the tank)** → lower fatigue per set → can run more weekly sets → volume accumulation strategy
- **Lower RIR (closer to failure)** → higher fatigue per set → must run fewer weekly sets → effort accumulation strategy

DPperformance picks the second path. We coach hard effort with capped volume. The reasoning:

- Clients have lives — recovery has a real ceiling outside the gym
- Hard effort produces a clearer dose-response — the client knows when they've trained
- Lower set counts fit a 3–5 day-a-week schedule in real-world time blocks
- The coaching language for effort is concrete and verifiable; "I trained at 3 RIR" is hard to verify, "I couldn't have done another rep" is something you can see on a form video

The cap matters. Pushing 0–1 RIR on 8 sets per muscle per session for 5 sessions a week is a recipe for systemic exhaustion. The set counts in Lesson 3.4 are deliberately conservative because the effort is high.

**Perceived failure vs true failure**

Here's the awkward truth: **most clients stop 2–3 reps short of true failure and call it failure.** This is consistent across the literature and across every coaching practice that's ever tracked it carefully. The brain is much better at protecting the body from "almost failure" than it is at finding actual failure. A client says "I couldn't have done another one" and means "the next one would have been very hard." Those are different things.

What this means in practice:

- A client reporting working sets at 0 RIR is probably training at 2–3 RIR
- A client at "1 RIR" is probably at 3–4 RIR
- A client at "5 RIR" is barely warming up

Without a coaching intervention, this drift continues quietly across the block. Progress slows, the client thinks the program isn't working, and the actual cause is that they've never trained at the prescribed effort.

**How to coach effort**

The fix is structural, not motivational. Three tools:

**1. Specific language during onboarding.** Don't tell a client to "go to failure" — define it concretely.

> "Failure on this set means the bar (or the dumbbell) physically does not move the next rep with the same form you've been using. Not 'feels heavy' — actually doesn't move. The set ends when you fail a rep, not when you feel like it might be the last."

**2. The form-video request.** This is the highest-leverage tool we have for verifying effort. Ask for a form video on the last working set of a key compound lift in the first 2–3 weeks of a new client.

> "Send me a video of the last set of bench press this week — just the working set, not the warm-up. I want to see what your top-end effort looks like so I can calibrate the program to you."

The video tells you everything. If the bar speed on the last rep is the same as the first rep, they had 3+ reps in the tank. If the last rep grinds for 4 seconds, they were actually close. If they re-rack with a smile and start the next set 30 seconds later, they were not at 0 RIR.

**3. The grind-rep cue.** Train clients to expect the last rep to be ugly.

> "The last rep on a working set should look ugly — slow, grindy, maybe you stall halfway through it. If your last rep looks the same as your first rep, you stopped early. The set isn't done until you've earned that last rep."

Most clients have never seen a grind-rep on themselves. They think failure feels worse than it does. Coaching them to *expect* the grind is what unlocks real working effort.

**Expected RIR by lift type — the working table**

Memorise these. They'll come up in every plan you write.

- **Compound 5–10 rep work** (heavy squat, bench, deadlift, OHP) → 1 RIR. Protect the spine, the joints, and the next session.
- **Compound 8–12 rep work** (moderate-load compounds, hip thrusts, rows in a hypertrophy block) → 0–1 RIR. Closer to 0 as the block matures.
- **Isolation 8–15 rep work** (curls, extensions, raises, leg work on machines) → 0 RIR. Take it to actual failure.
- **Machine work** (chest press, leg press, hack squat, lat pulldown, cable work) → 0 RIR. The machine is built to be safe at failure — use it.
- **Drop sets, rest-pause, triple drops** (advanced techniques in Lesson 3.4) → multiple points of 0 RIR inside the same set. These are by definition full-failure techniques.

The pattern: heavier and more systemic = leave one rep, lighter and more isolated = take it to zero. Neither end ever sits at 3 RIR.

**The coaching script for explaining failure to clients**

Use this verbatim with new clients in week one. It frames effort correctly and pre-empts every common misunderstanding.

> "Quick one on effort — when I prescribe a set at 0–1 RIR, what I'm asking for is a set where, on the last rep, you genuinely could not do another one with good form. Not 'the next one would be hard' — actually couldn't. On compound lifts like squat or bench, leave one rep in the tank for safety. On isolation work — curls, extensions, lateral raises, anything on a machine — push it to the point where the next rep doesn't happen.
>
> Most people stop 2–3 reps before they think they have. That's normal — the brain is conservative. The fix is the last rep should look ugly. Slow, grindy, maybe you stall halfway through. If your last rep looks the same as your first rep, you stopped early.
>
> If I see your numbers stalling on the log, I might ask for a form video on the last working set so I can calibrate this with you. That's not me checking up — it's how we find the right effort together."

Three things this script does at once: it defines effort concretely, predicts the common drift (the wizard principle), and pre-frames the form-video request as collaboration rather than surveillance. Adherence to effort climbs sharply once a client has heard this in their own coach's voice.

**The takeaway**

Hard effort is what makes the program work. Lower set counts buy us the recovery to do it. The coach's job is verifying effort exists — not assuming it does because the log says 0 RIR. Train the client to find their actual top end, and the rest of the system delivers.

lessons.title: Volume Framework & Stimulus-to-Fatigue Ratio
lessons.summary: MEV/MAV/MRV as a concept, why DP doesn't prescribe per-muscle weekly volume, and the S:F ratio as the lens for exercise selection.
lessons.body:
**Why this lesson is concept-heavy**

Volume is the most argued-about variable in hypertrophy programming. There are coaches who count every set per muscle per week and titrate it weekly. There are coaches who ignore volume entirely. DPperformance sits in the middle: coaches must **understand the volume framework deeply** so they can make better judgement calls — but we **prescribe by exercise, not by per-muscle weekly volume targets**. This lesson is the framework. The next lesson is how we actually write the plan.

**Volume landmarks — MEV, MAV, MRV**

Three working numbers, originally formalised by Mike Israetel and now standard across the field:

- **MEV — Minimum Effective Volume.** The smallest amount of weekly stimulus that produces measurable hypertrophy. For most muscles in most beginners, this is roughly **5–10 hard sets per muscle per week**.
- **MAV — Maximum Adaptive Volume.** The range across which more volume produces more hypertrophy, with diminishing returns at the top. For intermediate and advanced lifters, this is roughly **8–20 hard sets per muscle per week**, with the right number for any given person sitting somewhere inside it.
- **MRV — Maximum Recoverable Volume.** The ceiling beyond which fatigue exceeds adaptation — the body can't recover from the work fast enough to grow from it. Past MRV, more sets actually slow progress.

The relationships:

- Below MEV → no growth signal
- Between MEV and MAV → growth, with more volume generally producing more growth
- At MAV → optimal stimulus for that person at that point in their training life
- Between MAV and MRV → still growing, but with growing fatigue cost
- Above MRV → going backwards

These numbers are not bright lines. MEV varies with effort (higher RIR shifts MEV up — you need more easy sets to equal a hard set's stimulus). MAV varies with training age (advanced lifters have higher MAVs because they tolerate more). MRV varies with sleep, stress, food, and life. These are working brackets, not laws of physics.

**Why DP doesn't prescribe by per-muscle weekly volume**

If MEV/MAV/MRV are real, why don't we hand every client a weekly volume target ("12 hard sets per muscle per week, here's how it splits across your sessions")?

Three reasons, all practical:

**1. The client doesn't think in per-muscle weekly sets.** They think in "what am I doing today at the gym." A plan that hands them five sessions and 47 exercises with implied per-muscle math at the back is a plan that produces confusion. Adherence drops the moment the client doesn't understand the structure.

**2. The 1–4 sets per exercise framework is robust.** Most exercises in DP plans are prescribed at 2–4 sets. A client doing 3 sets of squat, 3 sets of leg press, 3 sets of leg curl, 3 sets of leg extension on a leg day is hitting roughly 12 sets between quads, hams, and glutes — comfortably in MAV for an intermediate lifter — without the coach ever counting per-muscle weekly volume. The structure produces a sensible total automatically.

**3. Every client's MAV is different and changes over time.** Counting weekly per-muscle sets to a target implies you know what the right number is. You don't — not exactly, not for this person, not this month. The coach's actual job is reading the data: are weights and reps moving up week-over-week? If yes, the volume is working. If no, ask why — and volume is one of several possible answers.

So coaches understand MEV/MAV/MRV as a framework. They use it as the *why* behind decisions. They don't use it as the *what* in the plan.

The mental model:

> "I'm not going to write '14 sets of chest per week' on this client's plan. I'm going to write 4 chest exercises across two sessions, each at 3 sets, and check that the load is climbing on each one. That puts him in MAV without him ever needing to know what MAV means."

**Stimulus-to-Fatigue ratio — the lens for exercise selection**

The concept that does the heavy lifting in DP exercise selection is **Stimulus-to-Fatigue (S:F) ratio**. Every exercise produces some amount of hypertrophy stimulus and some amount of systemic fatigue. The ratio between the two is the question.

The four quadrants:

**1. High stimulus + low fatigue → isolation and machine work.** Leg extensions, leg curls, cable curls, lateral raises, chest press machine, lat pulldown, pec deck, hack squat. Big stimulus on the target muscle, low systemic cost. **Excellent for volume accumulation.** This is where the back half of every session lives.

**2. High stimulus + high fatigue → compound free-weight lifts.** Barbell squat, deadlift, bench, overhead press, Romanian deadlift, barbell row, hip thrust. Huge stimulus across multiple muscles, but the fatigue cost is real — they tax the central nervous system, the joints, and the recovery budget. **Program these as the core of the session, in lower set counts.** Typically 1–3 working sets after warm-ups.

**3. Low stimulus + low fatigue → most cable accessories, machine isolation, light bodyweight.** Useful as finishers, as warm-ups, or as low-fatigue volume top-ups. Don't build the program on these, but they have a place.

**4. Low stimulus + high fatigue → avoid.** This is the trap quadrant. Examples: quarter-squats with heavy load (high systemic cost, minimal range-of-motion stimulus), heavy ego-pulled rack pulls (huge spinal load, low actual hamstring/back stimulus), upright rows for some lifters (shoulder fatigue with little delt growth), behind-the-neck pressing for most (joint fatigue, capacity-limited stimulus). Whenever an exercise is producing more soreness, joint complaint, or recovery debt than it is producing visible growth, ask whether it's a quadrant-4 lift for this client.

**Practical takeaway — how a coach uses S:F**

When you're writing a session, you're picking exercises from quadrants 1 and 2. Compound from quadrant 2 first (1–3 working sets on the highest S:F compound that fits the muscle and the equipment available), then accumulate volume in quadrant 1 (2–4 isolation/machine exercises at 2–3 sets each).

The quick decision rule: **does this exercise produce a clear, target-muscle pump at moderate effort, without wrecking my recovery for tomorrow?** If yes, it's high S:F. If you're sore in the lower back from "leg work," in the front delts from "chest work," or fatigued for two days from a single accessory exercise — the S:F is wrong, swap it.

**Putting the framework together**

The combined picture, the way an experienced DP coach holds it:

- **Effort sets the dose** (Lesson 3.2 — 0–1 RIR working sets)
- **Volume framework provides the why** (this lesson — MEV/MAV/MRV exists, we live inside MAV)
- **S:F ratio drives exercise selection** (this lesson — pick from quadrants 1 and 2, avoid 4)
- **The 1–4 sets-per-exercise rule produces a sensible weekly total automatically** (Lesson 3.4)

A coach who can hold all four at once writes plans that work for the right reasons. A coach who only knows the rule ("3 sets of everything") writes plans that work most of the time and break in interesting ways the rest of the time. The framework is what lets you diagnose and adjust.

**The TL;DR**

- MEV is roughly 5–10 sets per muscle per week for beginners
- MAV is roughly 8–20 sets per muscle per week for intermediates and above
- MRV is the ceiling beyond which fatigue exceeds adaptation
- DP coaches understand these but don't prescribe weekly per-muscle targets — they prescribe by exercise
- Pick exercises from the high-stimulus / low-fatigue and high-stimulus / high-fatigue quadrants
- Avoid the low-stimulus / high-fatigue trap
- The 1–4 sets per exercise structure produces a sensible weekly volume total without explicit accounting

lessons.title: Programming the First Block
lessons.summary: Frequency targets, the base splits for males and females, rep ranges by lift type, set count guidelines, exercise selection rules, and the substitution tier system.
lessons.body:
**The first plan a client sees**

This lesson is the practical build. After the philosophy, the effort frame, and the volume concept, this is how the first 4–8 weeks of training actually look on the page. Get this lesson right and you can ship a real plan to a real client by the end of the week.

**Frequency target — 3 to 5 gym sessions per week**

The default range is **3–5 gym sessions per week**. Below 3, the per-session work required to produce a hypertrophy stimulus is too high to fit in a real-world session. Above 5, recovery debt and time cost start outweighing the marginal gain. Inside 3–5, the right number is set by:

- **The client's actual schedule.** A parent of a toddler with a full job might genuinely cap at 3. A 23-year-old student can run 5.
- **Training experience.** Beginners thrive on 3 well-structured full-body or upper-lower sessions. Intermediates and advanced lifters need 4–5 to fit the volume.
- **The goal phase.** A cut sometimes reduces by one session if recovery is suffering. A build phase pushes toward the upper end.
- **Female prescription** — covered in detail in Lesson 3.5, but as a default, **female plans typically run 4–5 sessions** even when an equivalent male might be at 3–4. Women tolerate more weekly volume and benefit from higher frequency.

The baseline: ask what the client can actually commit to without their week unravelling, then prescribe at the top of that real ceiling — not at the top of a fantasy ceiling.

**The base splits — what's on the menu**

The DP standard split library, written so a coach can pull the right one off the shelf without re-inventing it.

**3-day splits:**
- **Full Body x3 (M/F)** — best for beginners, busy schedules, returning lifters. Each session hits the whole body at moderate volume per muscle.
- **Upper / Lower / Upper (M)** — male intermediate default at 3 sessions. Skews chest/back/shoulders.
- **Lower / Upper / Lower (F)** — female intermediate default at 3 sessions. Skews glutes/quads/hams.
- **Upper / Lower / Full Body** — middle path when the third session is "whatever fits."

**4-day splits:**
- **Push / Pull / Legs + Upper (M)** — male standard 4-day. PPL covers everything once, the 4th upper session top-loads chest/back/shoulder volume.
- **Upper / Lower x2 (M/F)** — clean, high-frequency split that works for almost everyone. Each muscle hit twice a week.
- **Glutes / Upper / Full Lower / Full Body (F)** — female-leaning 4-day with a dedicated glute session.
- **Lower / Upper / Lower / Glutes & Back (F)** — female 4-day weighting posterior development heavily.

**5-day splits:**
- **PPL + Upper / Lower (M)** — male 5-day standard. Covers everything once via PPL, top-loads upper and lower with a dedicated session each.
- **PPL Anterior / Posterior (M)** — for advanced male lifters wanting separated pulling and pushing emphasis.
- **PPL + Chest&Back + Arms (M)** — for clients with specific lagging-area focus.
- **Glutes / Upper / Quads&Glutes / Upper / Hams&Glutes (F)** — female 5-day with three glute-touching days. The default for serious female physique work.

The match: pick the split that fits the client's frequency, sex, and goal first. Worry about the specific exercises second.

**Rep ranges by lift type**

Memorise these — they're the targets you'll prescribe on every exercise.

- **Compound lifts** (squat, deadlift, bench, OHP, row, hip thrust) — **5–10 reps**. Heavier compounds at the bottom of the range, hypertrophy-leaning compounds at the top.
- **Isolation and machine work** (curls, extensions, lateral raises, leg curls, cable work, machines) — **8–15 reps**. Most isolations live at 10–12 in practice.
- **Higher-rep work** (banded glute work, cable abductions, calf raises, some shoulder isolation) — **15–25 reps** when muscle endurance and pump matter.

Rep ranges are prescribed as a range (e.g., "4 sets of 8–12") not a single number. The Dynamic Double Progression rule (Lesson 3.1) lives inside the range — climb it, jump the weight, climb the new range.

**Set count guidelines — the 1 to 4 rule**

Every exercise is prescribed at **1 to 4 sets**. The breakdown:

- **1 set** — used for advanced techniques. A single drop set, rest-pause set, or triple-drop set on an isolation can be enough volume on its own when the effort is high.
- **2 sets** — used either as a top-up on accessory work, OR as part of a top-set + back-off structure on compounds (more on this below — it's a common DP default, not advanced-only).
- **3 sets** — **the default for most exercises and most clients.** When in doubt, 3 sets.
- **4 sets** — reserved for priority muscles, primary compounds in build phases, or beginner programs where volume drives progress.

The decision tree:

- New client, 3 sets unless a specific reason
- Advanced client, often 2 hard sets (top + back-off) per exercise to fit more exercises in the session
- 4 sets only for the muscle group that's being prioritised
- Drop sets, rest-pause, or triple drops when 1 set is all that's needed for the stimulus

This is how the volume framework from Lesson 3.3 produces a sensible weekly total without explicit per-muscle accounting. A 4-day Upper/Lower/Upper/Lower split with 3 sets on each compound and 3 sets on each isolation puts an intermediate client at roughly 12–18 sets per muscle per week — comfortably in MAV.

**Top set + back-off structure on compounds**

For compound lifts, our default isn't 3 straight sets at the same weight and rep range. It's **2 heavy top sets + 1 back-off set at higher reps**. Same total set count, much better stimulus:

- **Top sets**: 5–10 reps (or 6–8 on the heaviest movements like hip thrusts, RDLs, hack squats), at 1 RIR. This is where strength and motor unit recruitment happen.
- **Back-off set**: 12–15 reps, at 0 RIR. Drop the load enough to hit the higher reps with full effort. This is where metabolic stress and additional volume on the same target lives.

Why this beats 3 straight sets at the same weight: the top sets push the heavy adaptation; the back-off captures the hypertrophic finish that pure heavy work can leave on the table. Coaches who've never used this structure are usually surprised at how much more effective the same set count becomes.

When to use it: compounds (squats, deadlifts, hip thrusts, presses, rows, RDLs, lat pulldowns, hack squats). When to skip it: isolations (run 3 straight sets at 12–15 reps, 0 RIR — the back-off doesn't add anything that another straight set wouldn't), and beginners in their first 4–8 weeks (they need to build technique on the same load before introducing weight changes mid-exercise).

For priority muscles, the structure can extend: **2 top sets + 2 back-offs**. You'll see this on the hip thrust in female programming when glutes are the priority — 2 heavy sets at 6–8 reps, 2 back-offs at 12–15. Same logic, more total volume on the priority lift.

**Exercise selection rules**

Three rules, applied in order:

**1. S:F ratio first.** Pick the highest stimulus-to-fatigue exercise the client has equipment and skill access to. A barbell hip thrust beats a bodyweight glute bridge. A hack squat beats a leg-press-machine-as-squat. A chest press machine beats a smith bench for an in-experienced client.

**2. Pattern coverage.** Each session should cover the major movement patterns the muscles need: a hinge or pull for posterior chain, a squat or press for quads/glutes/anterior, a horizontal and vertical press, a horizontal and vertical pull. Don't skip patterns.

**3. Equipment realism.** A "perfect" exercise the client doesn't have access to is a bad exercise. Build the plan from the equipment they actually have. Coach the client up the tier system as their gym situation improves.

**Substitution tier system**

When a client needs a swap mid-block — broken machine, equipment busy, gym change — use the **three-tier substitution system** so the substitution preserves as much of the original stimulus as possible.

- **Tier 1 — Same pattern, same load profile.** The closest possible swap. Barbell back squat → safety bar squat or front squat. Barbell bench → dumbbell bench. Barbell row → chest-supported row. Tier-1 swaps preserve the movement, the load, and the muscle target. Use first.
- **Tier 2 — Same target, different equipment.** Barbell back squat → hack squat or leg press. Barbell bench → chest press machine. Romanian deadlift → seated leg curl. Tier-2 swaps preserve the muscle target but change the movement and the load profile. Use when tier 1 isn't available.
- **Tier 3 — Different target altogether.** Reserve for emergencies. If the leg day machines are all in use and the client only has 30 minutes, you might swap a leg session toward an upper session and rearrange the week. Tier 3 changes the muscle target — only do it when there's no other option, and rebuild the week's volume to compensate.

The rule the client hears:

> "If something's broken or busy, don't skip it — swap it. There's a tier-1 swap for almost every lift. Send me a quick message and I'll point you at the right one. We don't lose a session because a piece of equipment is busy."

**Logging requirement**

Every set, every rep, every weight, every session — logged. The training log is the source of truth for progression. Without it, the coach is guessing on every week's check-in.

The non-negotiable from Module 1 ("log your workouts") is enforced here. If a client isn't logging, that's a coach intervention, not a coach acceptance. Reframe gently in week one, more firmly in week three:

> "I noticed last week's log was a bit thin. Every set logged is what lets me actually progress your program — without the log, I'm guessing on next week's weights, and we miss the small wins. Even a quick photo of a notebook works. Just need the numbers."

**When to request form videos**

Form videos are coaching gold but they're a specific tool. Request them when:

- New client, in the first 2–3 weeks of any compound lift (calibrates the program to their movement)
- Stalled progression on a compound (Lesson 3.1's week-4 reassessment) — the form video tells you whether they're losing tension, dropping range, or training short of failure
- A client reports pain on a specific lift (form video before changing the exercise)
- A new exercise added to a plan — first-week video confirms the cue landed

Don't request a form video on every set every week. It's overhead the client will resent. Use it surgically.

**The combined first-block prescription**

Putting it all together, the first plan for a 4-day intermediate male client looks roughly like this:

- 4 sessions per week, Upper / Lower / Upper / Lower
- Each session opens with a compound (5–10 reps, 3 sets, 1 RIR)
- Followed by 2–3 isolation/machine exercises (8–15 reps, 3 sets, 0 RIR)
- DDP progression rule on every exercise
- Form video on the compound in week 1, week 4, and any time numbers stall
- Log every set
- Reassess at week 4

That's a real, complete plan. Lesson 3.5 covers what changes when the client is female. Lesson 3.6 covers what happens when the block ends.

lessons.title: Female-Specific Programming
lessons.summary: The full gendered prescription, women's training physiology, the specific adjustments to volume, frequency, rest and selection, and example weekly builds.
lessons.body:
**The DP stance — full gendered prescription**

DPperformance programs female clients differently from male clients. Not cosmetically — actually differently. The volume is higher, the frequency is higher, the rest periods are shorter, exercise selection skews to glute and posterior development, and the assumptions about recovery and fatigue are different. This is not "the same plan with a pink banner." It's a different prescription based on different physiology.

The wrong version of female programming — the one we explicitly reject — is "men's program with the weights cut in half." That approach produces under-trained female clients who don't see the result they came for and quietly drop off after 12 weeks. The right version is a plan engineered around how female bodies actually adapt, recover, and respond to training.

**Female training physiology — what's actually different**

Three differences, evidence-supported, that drive every adjustment in this lesson:

**1. Greater fatigue resistance within a session.** Women, on average, recover faster between sets and between exercises within a single training session. They reach metabolic failure later than men at equivalent relative loads. Practically, this means shorter rest periods are tolerated and more total work can fit inside the same session.

**2. Faster between-session recovery.** Women, on average, recover more quickly day-to-day from hypertrophy training. The same session that requires 48 hours of recovery in a male client may be ready to repeat in 36 hours in a female client. This permits higher weekly frequency without recovery debt building up.

**3. Higher weekly volume tolerance.** Both effects above compound into a higher weekly volume ceiling. A female intermediate lifter typically thrives on 14–20 hard sets per muscle per week — the upper end of MAV — where an equivalent male might be in the 10–14 range.

These aren't absolutes. Some women recover slowly, some men recover fast. The default is what the default is, and the deviation is what the data shows. Coach to the default and adjust off observation.

**The specific adjustments**

Six adjustments, applied across every female plan:

**1. More weekly volume.** Where a male intermediate runs 10–14 sets per muscle per week, a female intermediate runs 14–20. The set counts on individual exercises don't change much (still typically 3 sets), but the number of exercises per muscle per week does — more lifts hitting the priority muscles.

**2. Higher frequency — 4 to 5 sessions standard.** Where a male might run 3–4 sessions, a female default is 4–5. The recovery permits it and the volume requires it. A 3-session female plan is reserved for genuinely time-constrained clients, not as a starting point.

**3. Shorter rest periods.** **60–90 seconds on most lifts.** Where male compound work runs 2–3 minute rests, female compound work runs 90–120 seconds, and isolation work runs 60–75. This isn't "to save time" — it's because shorter rests still produce full performance recovery in female lifters and they make the higher volume sessions actually fit in the time block.

**4. Glute and posterior emphasis on splits.** Female splits weight glute, hamstring, and posterior chain volume substantially. Examples from the split library:
- **Glutes / Upper / Quads&Glutes / Upper / Hams&Glutes** (5-day) — three glute-touching sessions.
- **Lower / Upper / Lower / Glutes & Back** (4-day) — dedicated posterior-finisher day.
- **Glutes / Upper / Full Lower / Full Body** (4-day) — opens the week with priority glute work.

The reasoning: glute development is the visible result most female clients are training for. Programming the priority muscle with the priority frequency (2–3 dedicated sessions per week) is what produces it. Two stretching, two pumping, hip thrust as a hero compound — the structure follows the goal.

**5. Exercise selection skewed to high-tension glute and hamstring work.** Hip thrusts and barbell glute bridges as primary compounds. Romanian deadlifts and seated leg curls for hamstrings. Bulgarian split squats and high-foot leg presses where stretch on the glute is the priority. Cable abductions, hip extensions, and banded work as accessory volume.

**6. Cycle awareness without cessation.** The luteal phase (the week before menstruation) commonly produces lower energy, water retention, slower performance recovery, and higher perceived effort on the same loads. Coaches **acknowledge this without pausing training**.

The right call:

> "You might find this week feels harder than last week — the loads might not move as well, you might feel a bit puffy, training might just feel heavier. That's normal in the back half of your cycle. We don't pause, we just expect it. Hit the plan as best you can. Next week typically feels lighter again."

The wrong call: skipping a week of training because of cycle. Skipping cardio, slightly relaxing intensity, accepting a missed PR — fine. Stopping training is not fine. The cycle is a permanent feature of the client's life; the program has to fit around it permanently, not pause for it.

**Example weekly build #1 — Female intermediate, 4-day, 12 weeks in**

A 32-year-old female client, intermediate trainer, mid-cut, training 4 days a week. The split is **Lower / Upper / Lower / Glutes&Back**.

Compounds use a **top-set + back-off** structure: 2 heavy top sets at 5–10 reps (or 6–8 on the heaviest lifts) at 1 RIR, then 1 back-off set at 12–15 reps and 0 RIR. Heavier loads on the top sets drive strength and motor unit recruitment; the back-off in higher reps adds metabolic stress and total volume on the same exercise without re-warming up.

**Day 1 — Lower (quad-emphasis):**
- Hack squat — 2 top sets x 6–8 @ 1 RIR + 1 back-off x 12–15 @ 0 RIR
- Leg press (high foot) — 3 x 10–15, 0–1 RIR
- Walking lunges — 3 x 10/leg, 0 RIR
- Seated leg curl — 3 x 12–15, 0 RIR
- Standing calf raise — 3 x 12–20, 0 RIR

**Day 2 — Upper:**
- Chest press machine — 2 top sets x 6–8 @ 1 RIR + 1 back-off x 12–15 @ 0 RIR
- Lat pulldown — 2 top sets x 6–8 @ 1 RIR + 1 back-off x 12–15 @ 0 RIR
- Cable row — 3 x 10–15, 0 RIR
- Lateral raise — 3 x 12–15, 0 RIR
- DB curl + tricep pushdown — 2 x 10–15 each, 0 RIR

**Day 3 — Lower (glute/ham emphasis):**
- Barbell hip thrust — 2 top sets x 6–8 @ 1 RIR + 2 back-off x 12–15 @ 0 RIR
- Romanian deadlift — 2 top sets x 6–8 @ 1 RIR + 1 back-off x 12–15 @ 0 RIR
- Bulgarian split squat — 3 x 10/leg, 0–1 RIR
- Cable kickback — 3 x 12–15, 0 RIR
- Lying leg curl — 3 x 12–15, 0 RIR

**Day 4 — Glutes & Back finisher:**
- Cable hip abduction — 3 x 15–20, 0 RIR
- Glute bridge with band — 3 x 12–15, 0 RIR
- Single-leg cable kickback — 3 x 12–15/leg, 0 RIR
- Chest-supported row — 2 top sets x 6–8 @ 1 RIR + 1 back-off x 12–15 @ 0 RIR
- Face pull — 3 x 15–20, 0 RIR
- Cable curl — 2 x 12–15, 0 RIR

Rest periods: 2–3 minutes between top sets, 90–120s on hip thrust and RDL back-offs, 60–90s on everything else. Three glute-touching sessions across the week, posterior chain in priority position, and the volume sits at roughly 18 sets/wk for glutes — the upper half of MAV for a serious physique-focused intermediate.

**Example weekly build #2 — Female beginner, 4-day, week 1**

A 28-year-old new client, no real lifting history, 4 days available, beginning of her first DP cut. The split is **Upper / Lower / Upper / Lower**.

**Day 1 — Upper:**
- Chest press machine — 3 x 10–12, 1 RIR
- Lat pulldown — 3 x 10–12, 1 RIR
- Seated cable row — 3 x 10–12, 0 RIR
- Lateral raise — 3 x 12–15, 0 RIR
- Tricep pushdown — 2 x 12–15, 0 RIR

**Day 2 — Lower:**
- Goblet squat or hack squat — 3 x 8–12, 1 RIR
- Hip thrust (machine or barbell with coaching) — 3 x 8–12, 1 RIR
- Leg press — 3 x 10–15, 0 RIR
- Seated leg curl — 3 x 12–15, 0 RIR
- Standing calf raise — 3 x 15–20, 0 RIR

**Day 3 — Upper:** (same shape, slightly different exercise selection — incline machine press, cable row, DB curl, etc.)

**Day 4 — Lower (glute focus):**
- Barbell hip thrust — 4 x 8–12, 1 RIR
- Romanian deadlift (DB to start) — 3 x 8–12, 1 RIR
- Reverse lunge — 3 x 10/leg, 0 RIR
- Cable kickback — 3 x 12–15, 0 RIR
- Lying leg curl — 3 x 12–15, 0 RIR

Beginner adjustments visible: machine-led upper-body work for safety and learning, hip thrust prioritised across both lower days, no advanced techniques, conservative compound selection. The DDP progression rule applies — week 2 she'll either climb the rep range or jump 2.5 kg on the lifts she handled cleanly.

**The frame for the female client**

Communicate the prescription clearly. Most female clients have been told their whole training life that they should do "lighter weights and higher reps" or "more cardio and less lifting." That's wrong, and it's the reason they haven't seen the body they wanted. The first conversation:

> "Your plan looks like a serious training plan because that's what produces the body you came for. Glute and shape development comes from progressive overload on hard compound lifts — hip thrusts, squats, RDLs — same as any other muscle. We'll be running you on more sessions per week and a bit more volume than the male equivalent because women genuinely tolerate that better. The cardio is its own job — we'll cover it separately — but the lifting is what changes the shape."

This conversation sets the entire training relationship. The client believes she's been given a real plan, the coach has named the why, and the plan delivers on its premise. That's the DPperformance experience for a female client.

lessons.title: Mesocycles & Reactive Deloads
lessons.summary: The 8 to 10 week block as the default cadence, the reactive deload trigger, the deload protocol, what changes between blocks, the PRS<4 protocol, and active rest.
lessons.body:
**The shape of training across months**

A single session is a workout. A single week is a microcycle. A connected stretch of weeks running the same exercises and rep ranges with progressive overload is a **mesocycle** — a block. Hypertrophy adaptations happen at the block level, not the session level. A coach who only thinks one session ahead writes plans that drift. A coach who thinks in mesocycles writes plans that compound.

DPperformance runs **8 to 10-week mesocycles** as the default cadence. New programs typically land at the 10-week mark — that's the working standard at DP. The block opens with a fresh exercise set or rep-range shift, the client progresses through the DDP rule for 8–10 weeks on those exercises, and then either a deload or a new block begins.

**Why 8 to 10 weeks**

The window matches what the literature and our own observation across hundreds of clients converge on:

- **Below 4 weeks** — the client hasn't had enough exposures on each exercise to actually progress meaningfully. Skill, neural drive, and weight on the bar are still settling.
- **4 to 8 weeks** — real progressive overload happening. Most exercises moving up in load or reps every week.
- **8 to 10 weeks** — the productive ceiling. Progression slows but is still real, and the client has built deep technical and neural familiarity with the exercises.
- **Past 10 weeks** — most exercises have stalled. The client has plateaued on this specific block. Continuing produces effort without progress, which is the worst combination.

The 8-week vs 10-week call:

- **8 weeks** when the block is intense, the client is in a deeper deficit, or recovery is at the edge
- **10 weeks** when progression is still clean at week 8 and the client has good recovery capacity — this is the more common case in lifestyle coaching

The default is closer to 10 weeks for a build phase and closer to 8 for a sharp cut.

**The reactive deload — when, not just how often**

The classical model deloads on a fixed cycle ("every 4th week is a deload"). DPperformance uses a **reactive deload** model — we deload when the client's data and self-report tells us they need it, not on a calendar.

The deload trigger: **2 or more of the following four signals**, sustained over a week:

- **Motivation drop** — client doesn't want to train, sessions feel like dragging through mud, the gym is no longer a place they look forward to
- **Sleep drop** — measurable sleep reduction, more disturbed sleep, harder to fall asleep, or harder to wake up
- **Performance regression** — weights dropping or reps dropping on multiple exercises across a single week, not just one bad session
- **Pain or persistent niggle** — a joint, tendon, or muscle issue that's lingering past 3–4 sessions, not a one-day thing

Two of those four together is the trigger. One alone can be a bad week. Two means recovery has fallen behind work, and pushing through it produces injury, illness, or burnout.

The reactive model is honest: it admits we can't predict exactly when a client's recovery will dip, so we watch for the dip and respond when it appears.

**The deload protocol**

Once triggered, the deload is short and structured: **4 to 7 days, 50% volume drop, intensity holds**.

The mechanics:

- **Cut sets in half across all exercises.** A 3-set squat becomes 1–2 sets. A 3-set isolation becomes 1 set. Total session volume drops by half.
- **Hold the load.** Same weight on the bar as last week. The intensity per rep stays high.
- **Rep targets stay at the lower end of the prescribed range.** If the range was 8–12, hit 8 — don't push for 12.
- **Same exercises, same split.** The deload isn't a new program — it's the same program, dialled down.
- **Same effort coaching.** Working sets are still at 0–1 RIR. We don't sandbag the effort, we just do less of it.

The duration:

- **4 days** if the client recovers cleanly — back to full program by the next session
- **5 to 7 days** if the trigger was severe (multiple signals strong, pain involved) — longer dial-down

The reasoning: cutting volume drops the recovery debt fast. Holding the intensity preserves the neural patterns and the strength. By the end of the deload week, the client is recovered, fresh, and ready for the next block. They don't lose strength — they lose fatigue.

**What changes at the start of a new block**

A deload (or a clean end of an 8–10 week block) is the trigger for **a new mesocycle**. The new block isn't a continuation of the old block — it's a deliberate refresh.

Two things change at the boundary:

**1. Exercise variations rotate.** Hack squat → barbell back squat. Barbell bench → DB bench. Romanian deadlift → seated leg curl + good morning. Cable row → barbell row. The pattern stays (the muscle target stays), the variation changes. This produces a fresh stimulus on the same target, restoring the dose-response that had flattened on the old exercise.

**2. Rep ranges may shift.** A block in the 5–8 range can move to 8–12. A block in 8–12 can move to 10–15. A block in 10–15 can move to 8–12 with heavier loads. The shift forces the client to find new working weights and rebuilds the rep-climbing curve from a new starting point.

We rarely change both dramatically at the same time. Either the variation refreshes and the rep range holds, or the rep range shifts and many exercises stay similar. Both at once is too much novelty and the first 2 weeks of the new block become learning instead of progressing.

**The PRS<4 protocol — the bad-day backup**

Sometimes a client shows up to a session genuinely under-recovered. Bad sleep, stressful day, getting sick, period symptoms, or just a flat day. Pushing the full plan in this state is how recovery debt builds and injuries happen.

The DP solution is the **Perceived Readiness Score (PRS)** check at the start of every session. Client rates 1–10 how recovered and ready they feel. If **PRS is below 4**, run the **PRS<4 protocol** instead of the full plan:

- **The compound movement only** — top set + 1 back-off set, or just 2 working sets at the prescribed RIR
- **Skip the accessory volume** — no isolation work, no machine accessories
- **Keep the load** — don't drop weight, just drop volume
- **End the session in 30 minutes**

This is a low-volume backup that preserves the training stimulus on the priority lifts without compounding fatigue when the body genuinely can't handle it.

The protocol is permission, not avoidance. A client running PRS<4 every session is not under-recovered — they're under-engaged, and that's a different conversation. The protocol exists for the genuine bad day, used 1–3 times across a block, not as the default mode.

**Active rest — 1 to 2 times per year**

Beyond mesocycles and reactive deloads, DPperformance prescribes **active rest periods 1–2 times per year**. These are deeper resets:

- **1 to 2 weeks long**
- **Unstructured movement** — walks, swims, yoga, hiking, mobility work, social sport
- **No structured lifting** — explicitly no program to execute
- **No tracking pressure** — calories loose at maintenance, no macros, no logging

The client takes a full break from the program. The body fully recovers. Old niggles resolve. Mental load drops. Then they re-enter a fresh block with renewed motivation.

When to schedule:

- **Holidays** — overlay active rest with a planned break (Christmas, summer holiday)
- **Post-cut** — after a 12-week cut and reverse, an active rest week before the next build
- **Career or life events** — a wedding the client is in, a major work deadline, a move

This is the longest break in the year. Without it, year-three retention drops because the client never gets a break and starts to associate training with grind. With it, the same client comes back excited and ready for the next year.

**Coaching script — communicating mesocycle structure to a client**

Use this in week one with every new client. Sets the entire training year up correctly.

> "Quick frame on how the training year actually runs. We work in 6 to 8-week blocks — same exercises, same rep ranges, progressively heavier each week. At the end of a block, we either rotate to a new set of exercises and rep ranges to keep the stimulus fresh, or we run a short deload — 4 to 7 days at half the volume, same weights — and then start the new block.
>
> You don't have to plan the deloads. I watch for them — if your motivation drops, your sleep drops, your weights regress, or you pick up a niggle, that's the cue and I'll call it. Two of those four together and we deload. That keeps recovery ahead of work and stops the slow burnout.
>
> Also — a 1–10 readiness score at the start of every session. If you're below 4 on a given day, we just do the main lift and call it. That's a bad-day backup, not a regular thing. Maybe you use it twice in a block.
>
> And once or twice a year, we'll schedule a proper rest week — actually off, no plan, just walks and whatever movement you enjoy. Usually around a holiday or after a cut. That's part of the structure too."

Three things this script does: predicts the deload trigger before the client experiences it (the wizard principle), gives the bad-day protocol a name so the client doesn't feel like they're cheating when they use it, and frames active rest as a feature not a guilt-inducing pause. The conversation is what makes the system run.

**The TL;DR**

- 8 to 10-week mesocycles as the default block length (10 is the working standard, 8 for sharper cuts)
- Reactive deload triggered by 2+ of motivation drop, sleep drop, performance regression, pain
- Deload = 4 to 7 days, 50% volume cut, intensity holds
- New block opens with rotated variations and/or a rep-range shift
- PRS<4 protocol = compound only, top set + back-off, end in 30 minutes
- Active rest 1–2 times per year, unstructured, 1–2 weeks
- The whole structure is communicated in week one with the wizard frame

title: Cardio & Recovery
