lessons.title: Female Physiology Depth
lessons.summary: The four cycle phases and their coaching impact, the cycle masking principle, low-body-fat hormonal cascade signals, gut and thyroid red flags, lab interpretation as a coach, and birth control implications.
lessons.body:
**Why this lesson exists**

Roughly half of a DP coach's client base is female. Coaching female clients well is not a "nice-to-have" specialism — it is core craft. The single biggest mistake new coaches make with female clients is reading their data through a male lens: a flat scale week is treated as a stall, a sudden 1.2 kg jump is treated as adherence drift, a luteal-phase mood drop is treated as motivation collapse. None of those reads are correct. They produce coaches who pull levers at the wrong time, panic clients unnecessarily, and burn through trust.

This lesson is the female physiology layer that every other module is read through when the client is female. It does not turn coaches into endocrinologists. It teaches coaches to recognise patterns, communicate them clearly, and refer when the pattern is outside scope.

**The four cycle phases and their coaching impact**

A standard menstrual cycle runs roughly 28 days, divided into four phases. Each phase has a different hormonal profile, a different fluid pattern, a different appetite pattern, and a different training tolerance. Coaches read all of those at once.

- **Follicular phase (days 1–14).** Oestrogen rising, progesterone low. Insulin sensitivity is at its highest, training tolerance is at its best, water retention is low, mood is generally up. This is the window where the client tends to feel strongest in the gym, recovers fastest between sessions, and shows the cleanest scale data. The coaching read: *if the plan is asking the client to push, follicular is when she'll push best.* This is a good window to anchor a PR attempt, run a hard training week, or expect the cleanest weekly drop on a cut.
- **Ovulation (~day 14).** A short window — sometimes just 24–48 hours. Many female clients report a slight strength peak. Some experience a one-day water spike or mild bloating. The coaching read: usually nothing changes — note it, don't react to it.
- **Luteal phase (days 14–28).** Progesterone elevated. Water retention is up, hunger is up (often markedly so in the back half), the resting metabolic rate rises slightly (~+100 kcal/day on average — small, but real), training tolerance drops, and mood frequently drops in late luteal. The scale will *not* read cleanly during this window. A client who has been losing 0.4 kg/week through follicular can hold flat or even rise 0.5–1.0 kg through late luteal *while still being in a deficit*. This is the single most-misread window in coaching female clients.
- **Bleed (days 1–5 of the next cycle).** Water releases sharply. Weight often drops 1–2 kg in 48–72 hours. Training feels easier as the cycle ends. The "stall" of the previous two weeks resolves itself in three days.

The principle a coach internalises: **a 2–3 week apparent stall during luteal that releases at the bleed is normal — it is not a fat-loss stall.** It looks like a stall, the client experiences it as a stall, but the underlying body composition trajectory has been intact the whole time. The water just masked it.

**The cycle masking principle**

Because of the pattern above, the only honest weekly comparison on a female client is **same-phase comparison.** Follicular week 1 is compared to follicular week 1 of the previous cycle. Late luteal is compared to late luteal. Bleed is compared to bleed.

A coach who compares this Monday's weight to last Monday's weight without checking phase is comparing noise to noise. A coach who pulls the calorie lever in late luteal because "the scale stalled" has just deepened a deficit on a client who was already in one — and will then watch the scale crash 1.5 kg at the bleed, where it would have crashed anyway.

The discipline: every female cutting client has cycle phase tagged on the check-in form. Coaches read the phase before reading the scale. Same-phase month-over-month is the real read. Within-cycle is direction, not magnitude.

The script for explaining a luteal-phase apparent stall to a client:

> "What you're seeing on the scale this week is normal cycle masking. You're in late luteal — progesterone is up, your body is holding extra water, and your appetite is higher. The fat loss is still happening underneath; it's just not visible on the scale right now because the water is sitting on top of it. Expect a sharp drop in the next 5–7 days when your bleed starts and that water releases. We're holding the plan exactly as it is. This is the cycle window we plan around, not against."

That script does three things at once: it names the phase (so the client builds the same model the coach has), it predicts the resolution (so the client doesn't panic in the next 48 hours), and it holds the plan (so the deficit isn't deepened on a window where the deepening would just produce hunger without producing fat loss).

**The low body-fat hormonal cascade**

A separate pattern, more serious, applies when a female client has been pushed to a low body-fat state for a sustained period — whether through a long cut, a contest prep, or a cumulative pattern across multiple seasons. The body responds to chronically low energy availability with a cascade of hormonal down-regulation. The headline signals every coach should be able to recognise:

- **Period loss (amenorrhea).** This is the single biggest red flag. A female client who loses her period during a cut is a client whose body is signalling that the energy cost has exceeded the energy budget. This is not "she got lean." This is the endocrine system shutting down a function it can't afford to run.
- **Reduced fertility, libido loss.**
- **Mood changes, sleep disruption, anxiety, low motivation.**
- **Thyroid down-regulation** — slowed metabolism, cold intolerance, fatigue, weight-loss resistance even at very low intake.
- **Gut function degradation** — chronic deficit + chronic stress is a reliable formula for IBS-style symptoms emerging in clients who didn't have them before.
- **Brittle nails, hair thinning, dry skin.**

The coach response to any of these in combination — particularly amenorrhea — is **not** "push through to the photoshoot." The response is: pause the deficit, raise calories to maintenance or above, escalate to Daniel, and refer the client to her GP for blood work. The DP system does not produce the kind of client who loses her period for the sake of a leaner photo. Coaching that drives a client into that state is coaching the program will not back.

**Gut and thyroid red flags**

Beyond the cascade above, coaches will see standalone gut and thyroid signals in female clients of normal body fat too. The flags worth recognising:

- Persistent bloating that does not track with cycle phase
- Irregular bowel movements (chronic constipation or chronic loose stools) that aren't tracking food changes
- Brain fog disproportionate to sleep and stress
- Cold intolerance — feeling cold in environments where she didn't used to
- Hair thinning, brittle nails
- Unexpected weight gain at maintenance, or unexpected weight-loss resistance at a properly prescribed deficit
- Persistent fatigue independent of training load

Any cluster of these — especially three or more together — is a referral to the GP. Coaches do not diagnose. Coaches recognise the pattern, escalate to Daniel, and refer the client to a clinical professional.

**Lab interpretation — recognise, don't diagnose**

Coaches will occasionally have clients who share blood work — sometimes from a routine GP check-up, sometimes from a functional medicine practitioner, sometimes from an old contest prep. The DP coach is **not** a clinician and does not interpret labs as a clinician. What a coach can do is recognise patterns that explain coaching difficulty:

- **Low free testosterone in a female client** trying to lose weight at low body fat — pattern: weight loss has been resistant, libido is down, mood is flat
- **Low T3 with weight loss resistance** — pattern: thyroid down-regulation under sustained deficit
- **Elevated reverse T3 in a client under chronic stress** — pattern: stress and under-eating both elevate it
- **Low ferritin in a female client** with fatigue — pattern: iron deficiency, common in female athletes

The coach response in every case is the same: name the pattern, write to Daniel, and refer the client to her GP or a functional medicine practitioner. Do not write "your free testosterone is low, that's why you're stalling" in a check-in reply. Write "this looks like a pattern that is worth your GP looking at — I'd like you to bring this in for a clinical read."

**Birth control implications**

Many female clients use hormonal contraceptives — combined pill, progesterone-only pill, hormonal IUD, implant, ring, patch. The relevant coaching point is that hormonal birth control changes the cycle picture in ways that matter for how the coach reads data:

- **Phase tagging often loses meaning.** Many hormonal contraceptives suppress the natural cycle, meaning the follicular/luteal pattern described above doesn't apply cleanly. The client may still bleed (or not) on a withdrawal schedule, but the underlying hormonal swing is flatter.
- **Water retention can be elevated overall**, and can shift abruptly when methods change.
- **Body composition can shift** with method changes — some clients add a kilo or two of water/tissue when starting a method, lose it when stopping.

The coach implication: if a client is on hormonal birth control, **cycle phasing is not a usable coaching tool.** Don't pretend it is. Read the data through photo trend, waist trend, and 4-week scale trend instead. The same-phase comparison principle becomes "compare across 4-week trend windows" rather than "compare follicular to follicular."

**The frame to carry forward**

Female physiology is not a footnote in DP coaching — it's a layer that runs through every cutting decision, every refeed conversation, every check-in reply for half the client base. The coach who reads phase before scale, who recognises the low-BF cascade and refers, who can tell a client at a luteal stall to hold the plan with confidence — that coach retains female clients for years. Lesson 6.2 takes the next layer: how the goal itself is set and how it links forward into the next phase, on every client, male or female.

lessons.title: Goal Setting & Phase Mapping
lessons.summary: The full DP goal-setting flow, progressive goal setting, visual checkpoints, timeframes, flexible adjustment language, phase mapping, and the 7-step coach flow.
lessons.body:
**Why goal setting is a coaching skill, not a form-fill**

A client who knows what they're working toward stays. A client who doesn't, drifts. The single most reliable correlation in long-term coaching retention is whether the client can name their next 8-week target without thinking — and whether they can name what comes after it. If both of those are unclear, the client is at risk regardless of how good the plan is.

Goal setting is therefore a coaching skill, not a form-fill at sign-up. The DP coach sets goals at program start, refines them as the physique reveals itself, and links each goal forward to the next phase. Done well, goal setting becomes a quiet retention engine — the client always has somewhere to go.

**Goals are flexible, not rigid**

The first principle: **goals adjust as the picture clarifies.** A goal set on day one — based on a starting scale weight, a couple of photos, and a brief intake conversation — is necessarily an estimate. The coach has not seen the client lose 5 kg yet. The coach does not know how the client looks at 58 kg vs 55 kg. The goal at day one is a working hypothesis, not a commitment.

That hypothesis is refined over the course of the program. As the client gets leaner and the structure becomes visible, the right end-point becomes clearer. The coach updates the goal accordingly — sometimes pulling it tighter (the client looks better than expected at 55, the final target shifts to 53), sometimes pulling it longer (the client looks better than expected at 53, the final shifts to 51), sometimes ending the cut earlier than planned because the look is already there.

Telling clients up front that goals are flexible is a coaching move. It removes the all-or-nothing frame. "Our starting target is X. We will refine that as we see how you look at the milestones along the way" — that one sentence prevents the client from collapsing emotionally if the day-one target was off by a kilo.

**Progressive goal setting — don't show the end too early**

The second principle: **the end goal is often intimidating, especially for clients with a lot of weight to lose.** A client at 90 kg who needs to be at 70 kg to look the way they want hears "20 kg" and feels demoralised. A client at 60 kg who needs to be at 52 kg hears "8 kg" and pictures a year of restriction.

The progressive solution: set an intermediate target first. Don't lead with the end.

Worked example: a female client starts at 60 kg, target lower 50s. Phase 1 goal — 55 kg. That's a 5 kg loss, achievable in roughly 8–10 weeks at a controlled rate. The client can picture 5 kg. The client cannot picture "the lower 50s" yet because she hasn't been there in years. At 55 kg, the coach reassesses visually — *what does she actually look like at 55? Does she look like she's done? Does she look like she'd look better at 53?* — and refines the next goal accordingly.

That phased approach does three things at once. It makes the first commitment small enough to feel real. It puts the second commitment behind a checkpoint where the client has already won once. And it preserves the coach's ability to refine the target based on actual visual data instead of a day-one guess.

**Adding timeframes — turning goals into urgency**

The third principle: a goal without a timeframe is a wish. A goal with a timeframe is a project. The DP coach combines weight + time in the way the goal is named to the client.

Working examples:

- "At your current rate we likely have about 4–6 weeks left to get you to 52."
- "If your weekend stays clean for the next two weeks, you'll see 55 by mid-month, and then we have a decision to make."
- "We're roughly halfway through this cut — about 6 more weeks of this rate gets you to the phase 1 target."

The timeframe is not a contract. It's a frame the client can hold. It creates urgency without panic. It makes the daily adherence question concrete — *the next 4 weeks decide whether I hit this* — rather than abstract.

**Flexible adjustment language**

When the milestone arrives, the coach has a real visual decision to make. Sometimes the answer is clean: target hit, look is right, end the cut. Sometimes the answer is more interesting: target hit, but more loss looks possible and would look better. The coach offers a framed choice rather than dictating.

Working language:

> "We've hit 55 kg, which is your phase 1 target. Honestly, looking at your photos today, I think another kilo would look incredible — your structure is showing up well and you're handling the deficit cleanly. You have two clean options. Option A: we end here, reverse for 3 weeks, and lock this look in. Option B: we run another 4 weeks, push for 53–54, then reverse. Both are good outcomes. I'd lean toward B because of where your physique is, but the call is yours and I'll back either."

That language hands the client the agency, but with a clear coach recommendation. Clients almost always respect the recommendation when it's framed as a real read of their physique rather than an impulse to push harder.

The pre-emptive version: if it's clear at week 6 of an 8-week phase that the original target is going to need refining, the coach raises it then — not at the milestone. "Heads up — at the rate you're going, we'll hit 55 by week 8, but I think your physique is going to want another kilo to land at the look you're after. Let's plan for that now so we can stage the next phase cleanly." Pre-emptive framing avoids the client arriving at the milestone, expecting closure, and being told there's another month.

**Phase mapping — link the current goal to the next phase**

The fourth principle, and the one that turns goal setting into a retention engine: **every current goal is named together with the next phase.** Always. The client's current goal is never the only thing on the horizon.

The DP coach speaks in phase chains:

> "We've got about 4 weeks left of this cut, then we'll reverse for 2–4 weeks back to maintenance, and then we'll move into a lean bulk to add some shape through your shoulders and back. The bulk is probably going to run 12–16 weeks. By spring we'll be ready to set up the next cut from a fuller starting point."

That sentence creates a 6-month forward arc. The client can see beyond the current cut. The current cut becomes a step in a larger story rather than the entire story. When week 7 of the cut feels hard, the client has somewhere to go after it — they're not just trying to survive the deficit.

The retention math is simple: a client whose current goal is the entire horizon will reassess their coaching subscription the moment that goal is hit. A client whose current goal is one stop on a 6-month chain reassesses much less often, because the next stop is already named and there's already momentum into it.

**The 7-step coach goal-setting flow**

Pulled together, the DP goal-setting process runs in seven steps:

1. **Identify the estimated lean endpoint.** From starting weight, photos, structure, history. This is the working hypothesis for where the client probably looks best — the long-arc target.
2. **Set the initial milestone.** A nearer, smaller target — typically 5–8 kg of loss for a cutting client, achievable in 8–12 weeks. Something the client can hold in their head.
3. **Reassess visually at the milestone.** When the client hits the milestone, open the gallery, compare like-for-like to phase start, and judge: does this look like the endpoint, a stop along the way, or earlier than expected?
4. **Refine the final target.** Based on the visual reassessment, refine the long-arc target. Usually it shifts — sometimes shorter, sometimes longer, sometimes about right.
5. **Add a timeframe.** Combine the next target with a calendar window: "we likely have 4–6 weeks left to land at X."
6. **Link it to the next phase.** Name what comes after the current goal — reverse, maintenance, lean bulk, mini-cut. The horizon is always named.
7. **Adjust based on fatigue and adherence.** If the client's adherence drops, the timeframe stretches. If fatigue is climbing, a diet break enters the chain. The flow re-runs every few check-ins.

That flow runs at program start, runs again at every milestone, and runs again whenever the picture changes meaningfully. It is not a one-time exercise — it's the structure the coach uses to keep the client oriented across a 6-month or 12-month coaching relationship.

**The check-in language that ties it together**

Inside the weekly check-in, goal-setting language shows up in three places: the read of the current week, the prediction of the next, and the closing reinforcement. Working examples:

- *Read:* "Scale at 56.4 today, which puts you about 1.4 kg from the phase 1 target."
- *Prediction:* "If your weekend stays where it has been, we'll see 55 in roughly 3–4 weeks."
- *Close:* "After 55, we'll reassess your look — I have a strong feeling another kilo is going to want to come off, but we'll decide together when we're there."

Notice the phase chain woven into the close. Even mid-cut, the client is being shown the next decision point.

**The frame to carry forward**

Goal setting is the DP coach's single biggest retention lever after the quality of the check-in itself. A client who knows where they're going, who has a near target and a far target, who has a phase chain that extends 6 months out — that client stays. Lesson 6.3 moves into the dietary edge cases that the goal arc has to be built around when the client's eating context isn't standard.

lessons.title: Dietary Edge Cases
lessons.summary: Vegan plan-building, religious dietary requirements (halal, kosher, Hindu, Buddhist, Ramadan), gut issues, food sensitivities vs allergies, eating disorder signal recognition, and two worked examples.
lessons.body:
**Why this lesson matters**

The DP default plan is a 3+2 meal-structured, animal-protein-anchored, controlled-carb-cycled template. It works for most clients. It does not work for all clients. A coach who can only run the default produces an awkward fit for the vegan, the observant Muslim during Ramadan, the IBS sufferer, the strict kosher client, the Hindu vegetarian, the FODMAP-sensitive — and that awkward fit costs adherence, costs results, and costs retention.

Lifestyle-first coaching means the plan adapts to the client's life. This lesson is the practical layer for adapting the plan to the most common dietary edge cases the coach base sees.

**Vegan clients**

The biggest constraint in a vegan plan is the protein floor. Our cut-phase target — 2.2 g/kg target body weight for males, 1.8 g/kg for females — is achievable on a vegan diet, but it requires deliberate construction. The protein density per calorie is lower than animal sources, and the amino acid profile is more variable. Build the plan around:

- **Tofu** — high-density, neutral-flavour, easy to swap into the same slot as chicken
- **Tempeh** — denser than tofu, nuttier flavour, slightly higher protein per gram
- **Seitan** — wheat-based, very high protein per gram (off the table for gluten-sensitive clients)
- **Lentils, beans, chickpeas** — moderate protein, higher carb, useful in carb-anchored meals
- **Edamame** — strong protein-to-calorie ratio, useful as a snack or side
- **Vegan protein powder** — pea, soy, blend (pea/rice/hemp). This is often the single biggest tool for hitting the protein floor — at least one shake per day is standard

Acknowledge to the client up front: a vegan plan tends to run slightly higher carbs and slightly higher fats than the equivalent omnivore plan, because plant proteins carry more carb and fat with them. That's a feature, not a bug — the plan is built around it, not fighting it.

**Long-term vegan considerations the coach should flag for blood work**: B12, iron, omega-3 (specifically EPA/DHA — algae-based supplement is the clean source), vitamin D, calcium, zinc. If a client has been vegan for more than 6–12 months and hasn't had recent blood work, the coach recommends GP-led panels rather than self-supplementing blindly.

**Religious dietary requirements**

Most religious dietary requirements are sourcing constraints rather than structural changes to the plan. The plan template doesn't need to change — the food list within it does.

- **Halal.** No pork, no alcohol-cooked dishes, animal protein from halal-certified sources. The standard DP plan structure works directly. The coach builds the food list from halal-certified suppliers and avoids alcohol-based marinades or recipes.
- **Kosher.** No pork, no shellfish, dairy and meat separated within meals, kosher-certified products. The standard plan works with sourcing — the coach avoids pairing dairy with meat in the same meal slot, and routes the food list through kosher options. For strictly observant clients, also flag the Sabbath as a fixed-meal day.
- **Hindu vegetarian.** Variations matter. Some Hindu vegetarian clients exclude beef but eat other meats; some are lacto-vegetarian (eggs out, dairy in); some are pure vegetarian (eggs and dairy in); some are strictly plant-based. **Ask the client directly which version of the framework she follows** rather than assuming. Build to her specific stance.
- **Buddhist vegetarian.** Many Buddhist vegetarian traditions exclude onion, garlic, leek, scallion, and chives ("the five pungent vegetables"). This is culturally specific — not all Buddhists observe it. Ask the client. If she does, the food list adjusts accordingly and most savoury recipes need substitution.
- **Ramadan / fasting periods.** This is the largest structural adjustment of the religious set. The client is fasting from pre-dawn to sunset for roughly a month. The plan shifts the entire feeding window into the non-fasting hours: a pre-dawn meal (suhoor) that prioritises slow-digesting protein and complex carbs to carry the day, and a post-sunset meal (iftar) that opens with light foods and works up to a full meal. Total calories and macros are maintained where possible. Training shifts to the evening, ideally 1–2 hours after iftar so the client trains fed. The coach who runs Ramadan well writes the entire plan template ahead of the month, frames the client up for the schedule shift, and adjusts cardio expectations downward across the month.

**Gut issues**

Gut symptoms — bloating, irregular bowel movements, reflux, abdominal pain — are common enough that every coach will work with multiple clients carrying them. The coaching layer is symptom management, not diagnosis.

- **IBS / IBD active flare.** Simplify the food list aggressively, reduce fibre temporarily, avoid any client-named trigger foods, drop training intensity if symptoms are interfering. If symptoms persist beyond 2–3 weeks, refer to GP / dietitian — coaches do not manage active inflammatory bowel disease.
- **FODMAP-sensitive clients.** Use a low-FODMAP DP plan template — replace garlic, onion, wheat, certain dairy, certain legumes, certain fruits with low-FODMAP alternatives. Garlic-infused oil instead of garlic. Spring onion greens instead of bulb. Lactose-free dairy or hard cheeses. The plan still runs the same macro structure; the food list is the swap.
- **Reflux.** Avoid late-night heavy meals, citrus, tomato-based dishes, spicy foods, very large meals before bed. Push the largest meal earlier in the day. Smaller, more frequent meals can help.
- **Food sensitivities (not allergies).** Pattern-recognise — does the symptom track a specific food consistently? Swap that food, run a 2-week test, see if symptoms resolve. **Do not run elimination diets without a registered dietitian.** Coaches can swap a single suspected food; we don't run multi-food elimination protocols on our own.
- **Active food allergies.** Refer to a specialist if not already managed. Build the plan strictly excluding the allergen — no exceptions, no "trace amounts are fine," no swaps that introduce contamination risk.

**Eating disorder signals — recognition only**

This is the most important paragraph in the lesson. **Coaching is not therapy.** A DP coach is not trained to treat an eating disorder, and attempting to do so causes harm. What a coach can — and must — do is recognise the signals and escalate.

Signals that warrant escalation:

- **Skipping meals to "save calories"** — particularly combined with extra cardio as punishment after eating
- **Extreme food rules** — fear of specific foods, "good vs bad" food language, panic at deviation
- **Daily weight obsession** — multiple weigh-ins per day, scale anxiety beyond normal monitoring
- **Hidden binge episodes** — disclosed late, often with shame
- **Excessive cardio beyond program prescription** — the client is doing 60+ minutes daily that wasn't asked for
- **Compulsive body checking** — repeated mirror checks, pinching skinfolds, asking "do I look fatter than yesterday"
- **Withdrawal from social eating** — refusing meals out, avoiding family meals, eating alone

The coach response is straightforward: **notice, escalate to Daniel within 24 hours, do not attempt to treat.** The escalation is followed by a referral to the client's GP, a sport psychologist, or a registered dietitian with eating-disorder expertise. The DP program continues only if a clinical professional clears continuation. Coaching alongside ED treatment is sometimes appropriate; coaching as a substitute for ED treatment is never appropriate.

A coach who tries to "fix it themselves" — push through the rules, talk the client out of the fear, ignore the binge — is making the situation worse. The most caring move a coach can make in this scenario is the quiet, immediate referral to someone qualified.

**Worked example 1 — vegan female cutting client**

Maya, 28, vegan for 6 years, female, target weight 56 kg from current 62 kg. Phase 1 cut, 12 weeks. Targets: 1.8 × 56 = ~100 g protein, ~1,650 kcal training day, ~1,500 rest day.

The plan structure:

- Meal 1: Vegan protein shake (30 g protein, blended pea/rice) + oats + fruit + flax
- Meal 2: Tofu scramble (150 g firm tofu) + greens + sourdough
- Meal 3: Tempeh + rice + roasted vegetables + tahini
- Meal 4: Lentil and chickpea curry with rice on training days, lighter on rest days
- Meal 5 (training day): Vegan protein shake + banana post-training

Coach notes: protein floor hits via shake-anchored bookends + tofu/tempeh main meals. B12 supplemented daily, algae-based EPA/DHA supplemented, blood work flagged for the 3-month mark. Cycle phase tagged on each check-in. Plan reads as a normal DP plan with vegan sourcing — not a special-case plan.

**Worked example 2 — Ramadan male cutting client**

Hassan, 35, male, observant Muslim, week 4 of a 12-week cut when Ramadan begins. Pre-Ramadan plan: 2,200 TD / 2,000 RD, 5 meals, training mid-afternoon.

The Ramadan adaptation:

- **Suhoor (pre-dawn, ~4:30 am):** slow-digesting carbs (oats), high-protein anchor (Greek yogurt or eggs if not vegetarian, cottage cheese, or whey shake), healthy fats (nuts, avocado), water-loaded
- **Iftar (sunset):** open with dates and water (cultural tradition + glucose recovery), 15-minute pause, then a structured first meal with lean protein and complex carbs
- **Post-iftar meal #2 (~2 hours later):** the second main feeding — lean protein, vegetables, smaller carb portion
- **Pre-bed snack:** light, casein-style protein if compatible, or low-cal vegetable snack

Training shifts to roughly 90 minutes after iftar, so Hassan trains fed. Cardio sessions reduce to 2/week from 3/week across the month — recovery is harder during a fast, the deficit pulls back slightly to protect adherence. Total daily intake holds the cut macro target where possible; if Hassan can't hit it, the coach adjusts to maintenance for the month rather than risk a hard breakdown.

Post-Ramadan, the cut resumes. The 4 weeks of Ramadan effectively act as a structural diet break — even when calories are well-controlled, the rhythm change, eating window shift, and recovery from the weekly accumulated deficit gives the body a meaningful pause. The client comes out of the month rested, with a renewed window for the back half of the cut.

**The frame to carry forward**

Dietary edge cases are not difficult to coach if the coach is willing to learn the constraint and adapt the plan around it. The DP system is multi-system pluralist — we don't force vegans into omnivore plans, observant clients into non-compliant food lists, or gut-sensitive clients into the standard food list. We adapt. Lesson 6.4 takes the next layer: when a situation is *outside* the scope of coach autonomy, what the escalation looks like, and how to know which is which.

lessons.title: When to Escalate
lessons.summary: The full escalation list, the boundaries of coach autonomy, the 3–5 line Slack escalation format, and two example escalation messages.
lessons.body:
**Why this lesson exists**

A DP coach has real autonomy. That autonomy has edges. A coach who escalates everything is over-burdening Daniel and Angus and signalling to the team that they can't run a client. A coach who escalates nothing is making decisions outside their scope and putting clients — and the company — at risk. The skill is knowing where the edge is.

This lesson is the explicit map of which decisions live inside coach autonomy and which live outside it. It is not a punishment list. It is a resource — once a coach knows where the edges are, decision-making inside the edges becomes faster and more confident, because the coach knows the senior coaches are actually backing the autonomy zone.

**Coach autonomy — what you decide alone**

The decisions a coach makes without escalating:

- **Macro adjustments within ±15% of the current plan.** Pulling 100–200 kcal from carbs on a stalled cut, adding 200 kcal to a lean-bulk plan with stalled lifts, restructuring the TD/RD split — all standard within-plan moves.
- **Training split changes.** Shifting a 4-day upper/lower into a 5-day push/pull/legs, restructuring exercise selection, swapping volume between body parts within mesocycle bounds.
- **Session structure modifications.** Adjusting set/rep ranges, exercise order, technique work, conditioning blocks within the program scope.
- **Check-in frequency changes for short-term medical reasons.** A client with a 1-week stomach bug who needs a temporary fortnightly check-in cadence, or an extra check-in mid-week during a hard phase. Short-term, coach-led.
- **Pauses up to 2 weeks for circumstantial reasons.** Travel, mild illness, work crunch — the coach can authorise a 1–2 week pause without escalation. Document it in the client file, set a return date, communicate to the client.
- **Plan substitutions.** Swapping foods, restructuring meals, adjusting cardio modality — all standard.

If the decision sits inside that list, the coach makes the call, documents it, and moves on. Daniel and Angus do not need to be in those loops.

**Always escalate — the explicit list**

The decisions that always escalate to Daniel (or Angus where appropriate):

- **Refund requests, any size.** Every refund — partial, full, prorated — runs through Daniel. No coach issues a refund unilaterally.
- **Significant client dissatisfaction.** A client expressing serious unhappiness with the coaching, the program, or the company. Even if the coach thinks they can handle it, the senior team needs to know.
- **Medical issues appearing in check-ins.** Chest pain, persistent injury beyond 1–2 weeks, sleep apnea signs, signs of cardiovascular issues, anything outside coaching scope. Refer to GP and inform Daniel.
- **Eating disorder signals.** Per Lesson 6.3 — recognise, escalate within 24 hours, refer to clinical professional. Do not attempt to treat.
- **Pause requests that look indefinite.** A client asking for an open-ended pause, or a third pause request inside 6 months. The pattern matters more than the single request.
- **Cancellation within the first 4 weeks.** This is retention-coachable territory if the coach gets it right; it's also a signal of an onboarding problem if the coach gets it wrong. Daniel needs visibility.
- **Cancellation after term complete.** The post-term cancellation conversation is run with Daniel's input — there's often a reverse phase or maintenance conversation that the coach handles, but the senior team is in the loop on the cancellation itself.
- **Disputed payments.** Any payment dispute — chargeback, missed direct debit not resolved in 1 attempt, billing query the client is unhappy about. Daniel handles billing-disputed conversations.
- **Anything outside documented scope.** If a coach is uncertain whether a decision falls inside autonomy, escalate. The error mode is escalating slightly too much in your first 6 months as a coach — not escalating too little.
- **Public or social media complaints.** A client posting publicly about their experience with DP, a tagged story or post that's negative, a review going up. Daniel needs immediate visibility.
- **Legal or compliance concerns.** A client asking for medical advice in writing, a client requesting a clinical claim, a contract or terms question, anything that smells like legal exposure. Escalate immediately, do not respond on your own.

That list is not exhaustive. The principle: if the situation involves money beyond the standard plan, medical scope, mental health scope, public exposure, or terminal client decisions, it escalates. If you're uncertain, escalate.

**The 3–5 line Slack escalation format**

When a coach escalates, the message is short, specific, and ends with a clear ask. The format:

1. **What happened.** One or two sentences. Names, dates, specifics.
2. **What you've done so far.** One sentence. The actions you've already taken.
3. **What you need from Daniel/Angus.** One sentence. The specific decision or input you're looking for.

That's it. 3–5 lines total. Not a long backstory, not a defensive narrative. Daniel and Angus read dozens of these a week — efficiency in the format respects their time and gets the response back faster.

**Example escalation 1 — refund request**

> *Slack to Daniel:*
>
> "Sarah Chen (active 6 weeks) is asking for a 50% refund. She says the plan didn't fit her schedule and she didn't get the results she wanted. I've reviewed her check-ins — adherence sat at 60–70% across the 6 weeks, photos show modest progress, she's reported feeling overwhelmed twice. I've replied warmly to acknowledge her message and told her I'd come back to her tomorrow with next steps. Need your call on the refund and how you want me to frame the reply."

That message names the client and tenure, names the request, names the coach's read of the underlying picture, names the holding action already taken, and names the ask. Daniel can respond in 30 seconds with a decision and a frame.

**Example escalation 2 — eating disorder signals**

> *Slack to Daniel:*
>
> "Heads up on Maya Jansen — last 2 check-ins she's mentioned skipping meals to 'save calories' and added 30 minutes of unprogrammed cardio after a weekend dinner. This week she's reported obsessive scale-checking and asked if she can drop another 200 kcal. I haven't replied to the macro request yet. I think this needs a referral to her GP / sport psych and we should hold the deficit at current. Need your read before I write back to her."

That message flags the pattern (not just one comment), names the trigger that escalated it (the 200 kcal request), states the holding action (no reply yet), states the proposed referral, and asks for senior backing before the response goes out.

**Internal note culture**

Beyond the escalation list, a culture point worth holding: write client notes in the file as you go. When the escalation lands a week later, Daniel and Angus can pull the client file and see the trajectory immediately. Coaches who keep clean client notes make escalations dramatically faster to handle, because the senior team isn't reverse-engineering 8 weeks of coaching from the check-in feed.

**The frame to carry forward**

Escalation is not weakness. It's structural respect for the boundaries of the role. A coach who escalates correctly looks like a strong coach — confident in their autonomy zone, clear-eyed about the edges, careful with the cases that warrant senior input. Lesson 6.5 closes the module on the broader version of this principle: what the DP coaching scope actually is, and what lives outside it entirely.

lessons.title: What's Out of Scope
lessons.summary: The full out-of-scope list, the boundary principle that knowing where to refer is part of the craft, the referral language coaches use, and two example referral scripts.
lessons.body:
**The boundary principle**

Lifestyle coaching is not everything. A DP coach's scope is real and meaningful — structured nutrition, hypertrophy training, cardio and recovery programming, weekly check-ins, behavioural support around adherence — but that scope has explicit edges. Outside the edges sit clinical, psychological, medical, and competition contexts that are not coaching territory.

The most important thing a senior coach learns over time is that **knowing where to refer is part of the craft.** A coach who recognises an out-of-scope situation cleanly, refers without ego, and stays in their lane on the rest of the case is a far better coach than one who tries to do everything. Trying to do everything produces clients harmed by amateur attempts at endocrinology, sports psychiatry, contest prep, and pharmacology. Referring well preserves the client's outcome and the coach's professional standing.

This is also what a serious profession looks like. Doctors refer to specialists. Lawyers refer to other firms. Therapists refer to psychiatrists. The boundary is not a weakness — it is the structural shape of competent practice.

**The full out-of-scope list**

The contexts that are explicitly outside DP coach scope:

- **Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs).** Steroids, peptides, hormones, SARMs, growth hormone, insulin, anything pharmacological used for performance or physique. We do not advise on dosing, timing, choice of compound, harm reduction, or post-cycle protocols. Refer to a hormone clinic or endocrinologist. Even on clients who are openly using — and some clients are — the coach's coaching is on the lifestyle/nutrition/training side only. We do not pretend to know what we don't.
- **Contest prep.** Competition bodybuilding — peak weeks, water and sodium manipulation, posing, federation rules, stage tan, depletion protocols — is its own sport with its own coaches. We do not run preps. If a client wants to compete, refer to a competition coach. Lifestyle coaching can continue alongside if appropriate, but the prep itself is run by the competition specialist.
- **Eating disorders.** Recognition only — per Lesson 6.3. Refer to GP, sport psychologist, or registered dietitian with ED expertise. Do not attempt to treat.
- **Medical conditions outside scope.** Cardiovascular issues, endocrine conditions (diabetes type 1, severe thyroid disease, adrenal disorders), autoimmune conditions in active flare, oncology cases, neurological conditions — any acute or chronic medical condition needs the GP first. Coaching may be appropriate alongside medical care; it is never a substitute for it.
- **Acute psychological distress.** Suicidal ideation, severe depression, severe anxiety, trauma response — refer immediately to a mental health professional and inform Daniel. Coaches notice and refer. We do not counsel.
- **Pregnancy or postpartum without medical clearance.** A client who becomes pregnant, or a client in early postpartum, requires OB/GYN clearance before any structured deficit. Maintenance-level coaching with light training is sometimes appropriate with clearance. Aggressive cuts, postpartum, are not.
- **Severely underweight or overweight clients with comorbidities.** A client at a clinically dangerous weight with comorbid conditions is a medical case first. Refer to a medical team. Coaching alongside is sometimes appropriate; coaching as the only intervention is not.
- **Legal advice, financial advice, and life coaching beyond fitness.** Clients sometimes try to widen the relationship — career coaching, relationship advice, financial planning. Politely decline and refocus on the fitness coaching scope.

**The referral language coaches use**

The language for an out-of-scope referral is straightforward. The coach is honest, warm, and clear about the boundary. The client almost always responds well — clients respect a coach who says "I'm not the right person for this" far more than a coach who pretends to be.

Three working components of a referral message:

1. **Honour the question.** The client raised something real — acknowledge it directly.
2. **State the boundary.** Honestly: this is outside what a DP coach does.
3. **Hand off to the right person.** Specifically — name the type of professional, ideally with a recommendation if you have one.

The general pattern: *"This is a real question and I want you to get a real answer to it. It's outside what I'm trained to coach on, so I don't want to half-answer it. The right person for this is [X type of professional]. Here's what I'd recommend you ask them: [the specific question]."*

That language is honest, doesn't undersell the coach, and gets the client to the right resource. It is not "I don't know" — it is "this is outside my scope, here is who you need."

**Example referral 1 — PED inquiry**

A male client, 7 months in, asks: "I've been thinking about starting on test. What dose would you recommend, and how should I adjust the plan?"

> "Honestly, that's a question I'm not the right person for. PEDs sit outside what a DP coach is trained to advise on — I won't half-answer it because the cost of getting it wrong is too high. The right person for this conversation is an endocrinologist or a hormone clinic — they can run your blood work, look at the actual clinical picture, and advise on whether and how. I can recommend a couple of clinics if that's useful.
>
> What I will say from the coaching side: you've made strong progress over 7 months on the natural plan. Your back, shoulders and arms are visibly bigger and your lifts have moved well. There's still real progress available naturally if you want to keep going on this track for another phase. But that's a separate decision from the medical one, and the medical one needs a clinician's input."

That reply does several things. It refuses to pretend on the medical side. It names the right resource. It validates the client's progress so far. And it leaves the door open without compromising the boundary.

**Example referral 2 — psychological distress**

A female client, 4 months in, mentions in her check-in qualitative section: "I've been having a really hard time the last couple of weeks — feeling really low, struggling to get out of bed some mornings, not really wanting to see anyone. I don't know if this is just life being hard or something more."

> "Thank you for trusting me with this — I want to respond to it directly rather than just keep moving through the check-in.
>
> Honestly, what you're describing is outside what coaching is the right tool for. The patterns you're naming — persistent low mood, not wanting to see people, hard time getting out of bed — are signals that a mental health professional should look at. I'm not the person to assess that, and I don't want to under-respond to something that deserves a real read.
>
> What I'd recommend: book a GP appointment this week, name what you've named to me, and let them route you to the right next step (often that's a referral to a psychologist or counsellor, sometimes other support). On my side, I'm going to ease the program structure a bit while you work this out — I'll send a simplified version of this week's plan that takes pressure off without losing the routine. The transformation work will still be here when the bigger picture is clearer.
>
> You're not alone in this and you've done the right thing by naming it. Please book the appointment this week."

That reply names the boundary, names the right resource, eases the coaching pressure without abandoning the client, and closes warm. The coach has not tried to counsel — and has handled the situation in a way that actually helps the client more than amateur counselling would.

**The conclusion of the module — and the course**

Module 6 closes the academy. Across six modules you have learned the philosophy (Module 1), the nutrition system (Module 2), the training system (Module 3), the cardio and recovery layer (Module 4), the check-in operating system (Module 5), and the advanced and edge-case craft (Module 6). The structure is now in your hands.

The job from here is to run this on real clients, with real lives, week after week. The plan is structured. The check-ins are structured. The decision trees are structured. Within all of that structure sits a real, unscripted human relationship between a coach and a client — and that's where the actual coaching happens. A DP coach who runs the system cleanly *and* shows up as a real person in the conversation produces clients who transform, stay, and refer. That is the whole game.

The final exam that follows pulls from all six modules. Treat it as the integration check — the place where the threads from across the course tie together. After it, you are ready to coach.

questions.q: In one phrase, what is our coaching philosophy?
options: Maximum results at any cost — transformations are the only thing that matters
Wellness-first coaching that prioritises feeling good over visible change
Lifestyle-first coaching that delivers structured progress without breaking the rest of someone's life
Contest-prep methodology applied to general population clients

questions.q: Which of the following correctly names the three non-negotiables that sit underneath every coaching decision?
options: Drive the transformation, protect the life, hold the relationship — never sacrifice any one for the others
Maximum deficit, maximum cardio, maximum compliance — the harder, the better
Aesthetic outcome, contest-readiness, federation criteria — the standards of competition coaching
Calorie counting, macro tracking, daily weigh-ins — the data-only approach

questions.q: A client asks for a steroid cycle plan and dosing advice. What is the correct coach response?
options: Provide a starter cycle and conservative doses based on industry standard practice
Share personal experience if you have it, then be clear that prescribing cycles is out of scope for a coach — point them to an endocrinologist or hormone clinic for medical guidance
Refer to a competition coach who can advise on cycle design
Suggest the client research it themselves and report back what they want to run

questions.q: How do we handle the macros-only request from an experienced client who doesn't want a structured meal plan?
options: Refuse the request — every DP client must follow a structured plan with no exceptions
Switch to macros immediately, with no further coaching expectation around adherence
Provide the macros conditionally — show us the logs, monitor results, gently steer back to structure if progress stalls, and respect autonomy if the client still wants macros after that
Charge a higher fee for macro-only coaching since it requires more frequent check-ins

questions.q: What is the protein floor for cutting clients?
options: 0.8 g per kg of current body weight regardless of gender
1.0 g per pound of current body weight regardless of phase
3.0 g per kg of target body weight regardless of phase
2.2 g/kg target body weight for males, 1.8 g/kg target body weight for females

questions.q: A male client at 18% body fat is starting a cut. What is the body-fat-graduated deficit guidance?
options: A larger deficit (≥600 kcal) — higher body-fat clients have more room to push
A moderate, conservative deficit — graduated to body-fat level, leaving headroom for adherence rather than maximising the rate
No deficit — train to maintenance and let body composition shift on its own
A 1,000 kcal deficit — aggressive enough to drive weekly visible change

questions.q: On a hypertrophy training session, what is the prescribed effort range and the volume principle?
options: 3–5 RIR, with very high volume (20–30 sets per body part per week) to maximise total work
0–1 RIR (close to failure), with capped volume — quality of stimulus first, total volume second
To-failure on every set, every session, with no volume cap
AMRAP-style sets with no defined RIR target

questions.q: In our training framework, what does the S:F ratio refer to, and why does it matter?
options: Sets-to-frequency ratio — the number of sets per session divided by training days per week
Strength-to-fatigue ratio — total weight lifted divided by perceived recovery cost
Stimulus-to-fatigue ratio — the productive training signal generated per unit of fatigue cost; we maximise stimulus while minimising junk fatigue
Speed-to-form ratio — bar speed relative to technical breakdown

questions.q: What is the default daily step target for an active cutting client?
options: 5,000 steps
20,000 steps
8,000 steps
10,000 steps

questions.q: What is the cardio ceiling — the point past which more cardio costs more than it returns?
options: 3 hours per week
5 hours per week
1 hour per week
10 hours per week

questions.q: In our recovery lever priority order, which lever sits at the top — adjusted before the others when a client is under-recovered?
options: Cardio reduction
Sleep — both quantity and consistency — sits at the top of the recovery lever order
Training volume reduction
Calorie increase to maintenance

questions.q: A female cutting client 10 weeks into a deficit reports her period has stopped for two consecutive months. She mentions feeling cold often, sleep is broken, and motivation is flat. Photos show she has leaned out further. What is the correct coach response?
options: Push through to the photoshoot — period loss often resolves on its own once the cut ends
Add a weekly refeed day and continue at the current deficit — the cycle should restore from the calorie spike

Pause the deficit, raise calories to maintenance or above, escalate to Daniel, and refer the client to her GP for blood work — amenorrhea is the endocrine system shutting down a function it can't afford
Drop training volume to ease the recovery load while keeping calories where they are

questions.q: On a slow-progressing but mostly-adherent cutting client, what is the correct lever order?
options: Food drop → cardio → high/low pattern → weekday/weekend split → TD/RD split
Cardio → food drop → TD/RD split → high/low pattern → weekday/weekend split
TD/RD calorie split → weekday/weekend split → high/low day pattern → cardio → food drop
High/low day pattern → food drop → cardio → TD/RD split → weekday/weekend split

questions.q: How do we treat refeeds and diet breaks differently before vs after 8 weeks of accumulated deficit?
options: Reactive only in the first 0–8 weeks (symptom-triggered); past 8 weeks, scheduled refeeds become structural and are built into the plan
Scheduled in the first 0–8 weeks regardless of symptoms; past 8 weeks they become reactive only
Always reactive — refeeds and diet breaks are never scheduled in the DP system
Always scheduled — every cutting client gets a refeed every 4 weeks regardless of phase

questions.q: What is our position on continuous deficit duration?
options: 12-week hard cap with a mandatory 1–2 week break, no exceptions
6-week hard cap before any structural break
No fixed week cap — symptom-driven breaks (sleep / mood / performance / adherence drops); exception is cuts targeting 20kg+, which get planned breaks every 8–10kg or 3–4 months
8-week hard cap with a mandatory 4-week break

questions.q: A female cutting client shows a flat-to-slightly-up scale through the back half of her cycle, with no adherence drift. What is the correct read?
options: Pull the calorie lever immediately — a stalled scale on a deficit means the deficit is too small
Add cardio — water retention is best resolved through increased expenditure
Likely cycle masking through late luteal — hold the plan, predict the bleed-week release, explain the phase to the client, compare same-phase month-over-month
Run a refeed week — the metabolic rate has adapted

questions.q: A client describes skipping meals to "save calories," adding unprogrammed extra cardio after eating, and hidden binge episodes followed by shame. What is the coach response?
options: Tighten the plan structure and increase check-in frequency until the patterns resolve through coaching alone
Drop calories further to reduce hunger cues and prevent the binge episodes
Wait 2–3 more weeks to see if the patterns self-correct before any escalation

Recognise the eating disorder signals, escalate to Daniel within 24 hours, refer to GP / sport psych / dietitian, and do not attempt to treat — coaching alongside continues only if a clinical professional clears it

questions.q: A client requests a partial refund 6 weeks into the program citing dissatisfaction with results. What is the correct coach action?
options: Issue a partial refund using the standard tier — refunds at this tenure are coach-autonomous
Refuse the refund and explain the no-refund policy within the contract terms
Counter-offer a free month of coaching to retain the client without escalating

Reply warmly to acknowledge the message, hold off on a final answer, escalate to Daniel using the 3–5 line Slack format with what happened / what you've done / what you need, and let Daniel make the refund call

questions.q: A new female cutting client mentions she's on a hormonal IUD with irregular withdrawal bleeds. The check-in form has a cycle-phase field. How should the coach read her weekly data?
options: Tag follicular and luteal phases as normal — hormonal IUDs don't affect how the cycle is read
Cycle phasing is not a usable coaching tool on hormonal birth control. Read the data through 4-week trend windows on photos, waist, and scale instead
Pause coaching until she comes off the IUD — clean cycle data is required to run a female cut
Use her bleed days as the only valid data point and ignore the rest of the month

questions.q: Which of the following best summarises the boundary principle for out-of-scope situations?
options: A senior coach should be able to handle anything a client raises, regardless of clinical complexity

Knowing where to refer is part of the craft — lifestyle coaching is not everything, and recognising clinical, psychological, and competition contexts that sit outside coaching scope is what competent practice looks like
Refer everything to be safe — coach autonomy is a liability that is best avoided
Coach autonomy is unlimited within the contracted relationship — the client signed up for coaching, so the coach handles whatever comes up
